on-anger_book-1.originalText: You have demanded of me, Novatus, that I should write how anger may be soothed, and it appears to me that you are right in feeling especial fear of this passion, which is above all others hideous and wild: for the others have some alloy of peace and quiet, but this consists wholly in action and the impulse of grief, raging with an utterly inhuman lust for arms, blood and tortures, careless of itself provided it hurts another, rushing upon the very point of the sword, and greedy for revenge even when it drags the avenger to ruin with itself. Some of the wisest of men have in consequence of this called anger a short madness: for it is equally devoid of self control, regardless of decorum, forgetful of kinship, obstinately engrossed in whatever it begins to do, deaf to reason and advice, excited by trifling causes, awkward at perceiving what is true and just, and very like a falling rock which breaks itself to pieces upon the very thing which it crushes.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: You asked me, Novatus, to write about how to calm anger. I think you're smart to fear this emotion more than any other. It's the most ugly and savage of all passions. Other emotions have some peace mixed in with them. But anger is nothing but action and the urge to cause pain. It rages with an inhuman hunger for weapons, blood, and torture. It doesn't care if it destroys itself as long as it hurts someone else. It rushes straight onto the sword's point. It craves revenge even when that revenge will drag the angry person down too. Some of the wisest people have called anger "brief madness" — and they're right. Anger has no self-control. It ignores proper behavior. It forgets family bonds. It stubbornly fixates on whatever it starts doing. It won't listen to reason or advice. Small things set it off. It can't see what's true or fair. It's like a falling rock that shatters itself on whatever it crushes.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: That you may know that they whom anger possesses are not sane, look at their appearance; for as there are distinct symptoms which mark madmen, such as a bold and menacing air, a gloomy brow, a stern face, a hurried walk, restless hands, changed colour, quick and strongly-drawn breathing; the signs of angry men, too, are the same: their eyes blaze and sparkle, their whole face is a deep red with the blood which boils up from the bottom of their heart, their lips quiver, their teeth are set, their hair bristles and stands on end, their breath is laboured and hissing; their joints crack as they twist them about, they groan, bellow, and burst into scarcely intelligible talk, they often clap their hands together and stamp on the ground with their feet, and their whole body is highly-strung and plays those tricks which mark a distraught mind, so as to furnish an ugly and shocking picture of self-perversion and excitement. You cannot tell whether this vice is more execrable or more disgusting.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Want to know that angry people are not sane? Just look at them. There are clear signs that mark madmen — a bold and threatening look, a dark frown, a harsh face, rushed movements, restless hands, changed skin color, quick and heavy breathing. The signs of angry people are exactly the same. Their eyes blaze and sparkle. Their whole face turns deep red as blood boils up from their heart. Their lips shake, their teeth clench, their hair stands on end. Their breathing becomes strained and hissing. Their joints crack as they twist around. They groan and bellow and burst into words you can barely understand. They clap their hands and stomp their feet. Their whole body is wound tight and does all the crazy things that show a disturbed mind. It creates an ugly and shocking picture of someone who has twisted themselves with excitement. You can't tell whether this vice is more hateful or more disgusting.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Other vices can be concealed and cherished in secret; anger shows itself openly and appears in the countenance, and the greater it is, the more plainly it boils forth. Do you not see how in all animals certain signs appear before they proceed to mischief, and how their entire bodies put off their usual quiet appearance and stir up their ferocity? Boars foam at the mouth and sharpen their teeth by rubbing them against trees, bulls toss their horns in the air and scatter the sand with blows of their feet, lions growl, the necks of enraged snakes swell, mad dogs have a sullen look—there is no animal so hateful and venomous by nature that it does not, when seized by anger, show additional fierceness. I know well that the other passions, can hardly be concealed, and that lust, fear, and boldness give signs of their presence and may be discovered beforehand, for there is no one of the stronger passions that does not affect the countenance: what then is the difference between them and anger? Why, that the other passions are visible, but that this is conspicuous.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: You can hide other vices and keep them secret. But anger shows itself openly on your face. The stronger it gets, the more it bubbles up for everyone to see. Look at animals — they always give warning signs before they attack. Their whole bodies drop their usual calm and work up their fury. Boars foam at the mouth and sharpen their tusks on trees. Bulls toss their horns and kick up sand. Lions growl. Angry snakes puff up their necks. Rabid dogs get that dark look in their eyes. Even the most naturally vicious animal shows extra feroceness when anger takes hold. I know that other strong emotions are hard to hide too. Lust, fear, and boldness all leave their marks and can be spotted ahead of time. Every powerful emotion shows up on your face. So what's the difference between them and anger? Simple: other emotions are visible, but anger is unmistakable.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Next, if you choose to view its results and the mischief that it does, no plague has cost the human race more dear: you will see slaughterings and poisonings, accusations and counter-accusations, sacking of cities, ruin of whole peoples, the persons of princes sold into slavery by auction, torches applied to roofs, and fires not merely confined within city-walls but making whole tracts of country glow with hostile flame. See the foundations of the most celebrated cities hardly now to be discerned; they were ruined by anger. See deserts extending for many miles without an inhabitant: they have been desolated by anger. See all the chiefs whom tradition mentions as instances of ill fate; anger stabbed one of them in his bed, struck down another, though he was protected by the sacred rights of hospitality, tore another to pieces in the very home of the laws and in sight of the crowded forum, bade one shed his own blood by the parricide hand of his son, another to have his royal throat cut by the hand of a slave, another to stretch out his limbs on the cross: and hitherto I am speaking merely of individual cases. What, if you were to pass from the consideration of those single men against whom anger has broken out to view whole assemblies cut down by the sword, the people butchered by the soldiery let loose upon it, and whole nations condemned to death in one common ruin . . . . as though by men who either freed themselves from our charge or despised our authority?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Now, if you look at what anger actually accomplishes and the damage it does, no disease has cost humanity more. You will see mass killings and poisonings. Accusations flying back and forth. Cities burned to the ground. Entire nations destroyed. Princes sold into slavery at auction. Rooftops set on fire. Flames that don't stop at city walls but light up whole regions with the fire of war. Look at the ruins of the most famous cities — you can barely tell where they once stood. Anger destroyed them. Look at deserts stretching for miles with no one living there. Anger made them empty wastelands. Think of all the leaders that history remembers as examples of terrible fate. Anger stabbed one in his bed. It struck down another, even though he was a guest protected by sacred hospitality laws. It tore another to pieces in the courthouse itself, right in front of a crowded forum. It made one man die by his own son's hand — his own child killing him. It had another king's throat cut by a slave. It stretched another out on a cross to die. And so far I'm only talking about individual cases. What if you moved beyond thinking about single men that anger has attacked? What if you looked at entire crowds cut down by swords? Whole populations butchered by soldiers turned loose on them? Entire nations condemned to die together in one shared destruction... as if by men who either broke free from our control or ignored our authority completely?

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Why, wherefore is the people angry with gladiators, and so unjust as to think itself wronged if they do not die cheerfully? It thinks itself scorned, and by looks, gestures, and excitement turns itself from a mere spectator into an adversary. Everything of this sort is not anger, but the semblance of anger, like that of boys who want to beat the ground when they have fallen upon it, and who often do not even know why they are angry, but are merely angry without any reason or having received any injury, yet not without some semblance of injury received, or without some wish to exact a penalty for it. Thus they are deceived by the likeness of blows, and are appeased by the pretended tears of those who deprecate their wrath, and thus an unreal grief is healed by an unreal revenge.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Why do crowds get angry at gladiators? Why do they feel cheated when the fighters don't die happily? The crowd feels insulted and turns from spectator to enemy through looks, gestures, and shouting. But this isn't real anger — it's fake anger, like children who want to hit the ground after they fall on it. Kids often don't even know why they're mad. They're just angry for no reason, without being hurt at all. But they still act like they've been wronged and want revenge. They're fooled by what looks like real harm. They calm down when people pretend to cry and beg for forgiveness. So fake grief gets healed by fake revenge.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "We often are angry," says our adversary, "not with men who have hurt us, but with men who are going to hurt us: so you may be sure that anger is not born of injury." It is true that we are angry with those who are going to hurt us, but they do already hurt us in intention, and one who is going to do an injury is already doing it. "The weakest of men," argues he, "are often angry with the most powerful: so you may be sure that anger is not a desire to punish their antagonist—for men do not desire to punish him when they cannot hope to do so." In the first place, I spoke of a desire to inflict punishment, not a power to do so: now men desire even what they cannot obtain. In the next place, no one is so low in station as not to be able to hope to inflict punishment even upon the greatest of men: we all are powerful for mischief. Aristotle's definition differs little from mine: for he declares anger to be a desire to repay suffering. It would be a long task to examine the differences between his definition and mine: it may be urged against both of them that wild beasts become angry without being excited by injury, and without any idea of punishing others or requiting them with pain: for, even though they do these things, these are not what they aim at doing.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "We often get angry," says my opponent, "not just with people who have hurt us, but with people who are going to hurt us. So clearly anger doesn't come from actual injury." True, we do get angry with those who plan to hurt us. But they are already hurting us with their intentions. Someone who is about to do you wrong is already doing it. "The weakest people," he argues, "often get angry with the most powerful. So anger can't be a desire to punish your enemy — after all, people don't want to punish someone when they have no hope of succeeding." First, I talked about the desire to punish, not the power to do it. People want things they can't have all the time. Second, no one is so powerless that they can't hope to hurt even the mightiest person. We're all capable of causing trouble. Aristotle's definition is close to mine. He says anger is a desire to pay back suffering. It would take too long to compare his definition with mine. But here's a problem with both: wild animals get angry without being injured first, and without any thought of punishing others or making them suffer. Even though they do attack and cause pain, that's not their goal.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: We must admit, however, that neither wild beasts nor any other creature except man is subject to anger: for, whilst anger is the foe of reason, it nevertheless does not arise in any place where reason cannot dwell. Wild beasts have impulses, fury, cruelty, combativeness: they have not anger any more than they have luxury: yet they indulge in some pleasures with less self-control than human beings. Do not believe the poet who says: "The boar his wrath forgets, the stag forgets the hounds. The bear forgets how 'midst the herd he leaped with frantic bounds." When he speaks of beasts being angry he means that they are excited, roused up: for indeed they know no more how to be angry than they know how to pardon. Dumb creatures have not human feelings, but have certain impulses which resemble them: for if it were not so, if they could feel love and hate, they would likewise be capable of friendship and enmity, of disagreement and agreement. Some traces of these qualities exist even in them, though properly all of them, whether good or bad, belong to the human breast alone.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: We have to admit that no wild animals or other creatures get angry — only humans do. Anger is the enemy of reason, and it can only exist where reason lives. Wild beasts have impulses, fury, cruelty, and a fighting spirit. But they don't have anger any more than they have luxury. Yet they do indulge in some pleasures with less self-control than we do. Don't believe the poet who says: "The boar forgets his wrath, the stag forgets the hounds. The bear forgets how he leaped through the herd in frantic bounds." When he talks about angry beasts, he just means they're excited and stirred up. They know no more about being angry than they do about forgiving. Animals don't have human emotions, but they do have certain impulses that look similar. If they weren't like this — if they could really feel love and hate — then they would also be capable of friendship and hatred, of disagreement and harmony. You can see traces of these qualities in them, but all of these feelings, whether good or bad, truly belong only to the human heart.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: To no creature besides man has been given wisdom, foresight, industry, and reflexion. To animals not only human virtues but even human vices are forbidden: their whole constitution, mental and bodily, is unlike that of human beings: in them the royal and leading principle is drawn from another source, as, for instance, they possess a voice, yet not a clear one, but indistinct and incapable of forming words: a tongue, but one which is fettered and not sufficiently nimble for complex movements: so, too, they possess intellect, the greatest attribute of all, but in a rough and inexact condition. It is, consequently, able to grasp those visions and semblances which rouse it to action, but only in a cloudy and indistinct fashion. It follows from this that their impulses and outbreaks are violent, and that they do not feel fear, anxieties, grief, or anger, but some semblances of these feelings: wherefore they quickly drop them and adopt the converse of them: they graze after showing the most vehement rage and terror, and after frantic bellowing and plunging they straightway sink into quiet sleep.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Only humans have been given wisdom, planning, hard work, and deep thinking. Animals can't have human virtues or even human vices. Their minds and bodies work completely differently from ours. Their ruling principle comes from somewhere else entirely. For example, they have voices, but not clear ones — just rough sounds that can't form words. They have tongues, but ones that are clumsy and can't make complex movements. Most importantly, they have minds, but crude and imprecise ones. These minds can grasp images and impressions that stir them to action, but only dimly and unclearly. This is why their impulses and outbursts are so violent, and why they don't really feel fear, worry, grief, or anger — just rough copies of these emotions. That's why they drop these feelings so quickly and switch to the opposite. A cow will graze peacefully right after showing fierce rage and terror. After wild bellowing and thrashing, animals fall straight into quiet sleep.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
What anger is has been sufficiently explained. The difference
between it and irascibility is evident: it is the same as that
between a drunken man and a drunkard; between a frightened man and
a coward. It is possible for an angry man not to be irascible; an
irascible man may sometimes not be angry. I shall omit the other
varieties of anger, which the Greeks distinguish by various names,
because we have no distinctive words for them in our language,
although we call men bitter, and harsh, and also peevish, frantic,
clamorous, surly, and fierce: all of which are different forms of
irascibility. Among these you may class sulkiness, a refined form
of irascibility; for there are some sorts of anger which go no
further than noise, while some are as lasting as they are common:
some are fierce in deed, but inclined to be sparing of words: some
expend themselves in bitter words and curses: some do not go beyond
complaining and turning one’s back: some are great, deep-seated,
and brood within a man: there are a thousand other forms of a
multiform evil.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: I've explained what anger is well enough. The difference between anger and being an angry person is clear. It's like the difference between being drunk and being a drunkard, or between being scared and being a coward. You can get angry without being an angry person by nature. And someone with an angry nature might not be angry right now. I won't list all the other types of anger that the Greeks name differently, since we don't have specific words for them in Latin. But we do call people bitter, harsh, cranky, wild, loud, surly, and fierce. These are all different forms of having an angry nature. You can add sulking to this list — it's anger in a more refined form. Some kinds of anger are all noise and nothing else. Others last as long as they are common. Some are violent in action but use few words. Others pour themselves out in bitter words and curses. Some don't go beyond complaining and giving people the cold shoulder. Others are deep, serious, and fester inside a person. There are a thousand other forms of this many-faced evil.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
We have now finished our enquiry as to what anger is, whether
it exists in any other creature besides man, what the difference
is between it and irascibility, and how many forms it possesses.
Let us now enquire whether anger be in accordance with nature, and
whether it be useful and worth entertaining in some measure.

Whether it be according to nature will become evident if we consider
man’s nature, than which what is more gentle while it is in its
proper condition? Yet what is more cruel than anger? What is more
affectionate to others than man? Yet what is more savage against
them than anger? Mankind is born for mutual assistance, anger for
mutual ruin: the former loves society, the latter estrangement. The
one loves to do good, the other to do harm; the one to help even
strangers, the other to attack even its dearest friends. The one
is ready even to sacrifice itself for the good of others, the other
to plunge into peril provided it drags others with it. Who, then,
can be more ignorant of nature than he who classes this cruel and
hurtful vice as belonging to her best and most polished work? Anger,
as we have said, is eager to punish; and that such a desire should
exist in man’s peaceful breast is least of all according to his
nature; for human life is founded on benefits and harmony, and is
bound together into an alliance for the common help of all, not by
terror, but by love towards one another.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
We've finished looking at what anger is, whether animals other than humans feel it, how it differs from being quick-tempered, and what forms it takes. Now let's ask whether anger is natural, and whether it's useful and worth keeping around to some degree.

To see if anger is natural, we need to look at human nature itself. What creature is more gentle when it's in its proper state? Yet what is crueler than anger? What is more loving toward others than humans? Yet what is more savage toward them than anger? We're born to help each other — anger exists to destroy each other. Human nature loves community, anger loves isolation. One wants to do good, the other wants to harm. One helps even strangers, the other attacks even close friends. One is ready to sacrifice itself for others' benefit, the other will throw itself into danger as long as it drags others down too. Who could be more ignorant about nature than someone who thinks this cruel and destructive vice belongs to nature's best and most refined creation? Anger, as we've said, is eager to punish. But such a desire has no place in the peaceful human heart — it goes against our very nature. Human life is built on kindness and harmony. We're bound together in partnership to help each other, not through fear, but through love.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "What, then? Is not correction sometimes necessary?" Of course it is; but with discretion, not with anger; for it does not injure, but heals under the guise of injury. We char crooked spearshafts to straighten them, and force them by driving in wedges, not in order to break them, but to take the bends out of them; and, in like manner, by applying pain to the body or mind we correct dispositions which have been rendered crooked by vice. So the physician at first, when dealing with slight disorders, tries not to make much change in his patient's daily habits, to regulate his food, drink, and exercise, and to improve his health merely by altering the order in which he takes them. The next step is to see whether an alteration in their amount will be of service. If neither alteration of the order or of the amount is of use, he cuts off some and reduces others. If even this does not answer, he forbids food, and disburdens the body by fasting. If milder remedies have proved useless he opens a vein; if the extremities are injuring the body and infecting it with disease he lays his hands upon the limbs; yet none of his treatment is considered harsh if its result is to give health.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "What then? Isn't correction sometimes necessary?" Of course it is. But we need wisdom, not anger. True correction doesn't harm — it heals, even when it seems to hurt. We heat crooked spear shafts to straighten them. We use wedges to force them into shape. We're not trying to break them. We're trying to remove the bends. In the same way, we use pain on the body or mind to correct bad habits caused by vice. A doctor works the same way. When dealing with minor problems, he first tries small changes. He adjusts his patient's food, drink, and exercise. He improves health just by changing the order of these things. Next, he tries changing the amounts. If changing the order or amounts doesn't work, he cuts some things out entirely. If that still doesn't help, he stops food completely. He makes the body heal through fasting. If gentle remedies fail, he opens a vein. If diseased limbs are poisoning the whole body, he removes them. None of this treatment seems harsh when the result is health.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Similarly, it is the duty of the chief administrator of the laws, or the ruler of a state, to correct ill-disposed men, as long as he is able, with words, and even with gentle ones, that he may persuade them to do what they ought, inspire them with a love of honour and justice, and cause them to hate vice and set store upon virtue. He must then pass on to severer language, still confining himself to advising and reprimanding; last of all he must betake himself to punishments, yet still making them slight and temporary. He ought to assign extreme punishments only to extreme crimes, that no one may die unless it be even to the criminal's own advantage that he should die. He will differ from the physician in one point alone; for whereas physicians render it easy to die for those to whom they cannot grant the boon of life, he will drive the condemned out of life with ignominy and disgrace, not because he takes pleasure in any man's being punished, for the wise man is far from such inhuman ferocity, but that they may be a warning to all men, and that, since they would not be useful when alive, the state may at any rate profit by their death.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: In the same way, a chief judge or ruler has a duty to correct wrongdoers. First, he should use words — gentle ones if possible. He wants to persuade them to do what's right, inspire them to love honor and justice, and make them hate vice while valuing virtue. If that doesn't work, he should use stronger language, still just advising and scolding. Only as a last resort should he turn to punishment, and even then it should be mild and temporary. He should reserve the harshest punishments for the worst crimes. No one should die unless their death actually benefits even them. The ruler differs from a doctor in one way: while doctors make dying easy for patients they cannot save, the ruler must drive criminals from life with shame and disgrace. This isn't because he enjoys seeing anyone punished — a wise person is far from such inhuman cruelty. Rather, their punishment serves as a warning to everyone else. Since they couldn't be useful while alive, at least the state can benefit from their death.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: Man's nature is not, therefore, desirous of inflicting punishment; neither, therefore, is anger in accordance with man's nature, because that is desirous of inflicting punishment. I will also adduce Plato's argument—for what harm is there in using other men's arguments, so far as they are on our side? "A good man," says he, "does not do any hurt: it is only punishment which hurts. Punishment, therefore, does not accord with a good man: wherefore anger does not do so either, because punishment and anger accord one with another. If a good man takes no pleasure in punishment, he will also take no pleasure in that state of mind to which punishment gives pleasure: consequently anger is not natural to man."
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Human nature doesn't want to punish others. Since anger makes us want to punish, anger goes against human nature. Let me also use Plato's argument — why not borrow from others when they support our point? Plato says, "A good person doesn't hurt anyone. Only punishment hurts people. So punishment doesn't fit with being good. Therefore, anger doesn't fit either, since anger and punishment go together." If a good person finds no joy in punishing others, then they also find no joy in the feeling that makes punishment enjoyable. So anger isn't natural to humans.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: May it not be that, although anger be not natural, it may be right to adopt it, because it often proves useful? It rouses the spirit and excites it; and courage does nothing grand in war without it, unless its flame be supplied from this source; this is the goad which stirs up bold men and sends them to encounter perils. Some therefore consider it to be best to control anger, not to banish it utterly, but to cut off its extravagances, and force it to keep within useful bounds, so as to retain that part of it without which action will become languid and all strength and activity of mind will die away.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Maybe anger isn't natural, but shouldn't we still use it because it's often helpful? It fires up the spirit and gets us excited. Courage can't do anything great in war without anger — unless that flame comes from this source. It's the prod that stirs up brave men and sends them into danger. So some people think it's best to control anger, not get rid of it completely. They say we should cut off its worst parts and force it to stay within useful limits. That way we keep the part of anger we need — because without it, action becomes weak and all our mental strength and energy dies away.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: In the first place, it is easier to banish dangerous passions than to rule them; it is easier not to admit them than to keep them in order when admitted; for when they have established themselves in possession of the mind they are more powerful than the lawful ruler, and will in no wise permit themselves to be weakened or abridged. In the next place, Reason herself, who holds the reins, is only strong while she remains apart from the passions; if she mixes and befouls herself with them she becomes no longer able to restrain those whom she might once have cleared out of her path; for the mind, when once excited and shaken up, goes whither the passions drive it. There are certain things whose beginnings lie in our own power, but which, when developed, drag us along by their own force and leave us no retreat. Those who have flung themselves over a precipice have no control over their movements, nor can they stop or slacken their pace when once started, for their own headlong and irremediable rashness has left no room for either reflexion or remorse, and they cannot help going to lengths which they might have avoided. So, also, the mind, when it has abandoned itself to anger, love, or any other passion, is unable to check itself: its own weight and the downward tendency of vices must needs carry the man off and hurl him into the lowest depth.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: First, it's easier to keep dangerous emotions out completely than to try controlling them once they're in. It's easier to refuse them entry than to manage them after they've moved in. Once they've taken over your mind, they become stronger than you are. They won't let you weaken them or cut them back. Second, Reason herself — the part that's supposed to be in charge — is only strong when she stays separate from the passions. If she mixes with them and gets dirty, she can no longer hold back the emotions she once could have kicked out entirely. Once your mind gets stirred up and shaken, it goes wherever the passions drag it. Some things start under our control, but once they develop, they pull us along with their own force and give us no way back. People who throw themselves off a cliff can't control how they fall. They can't stop or slow down once they've started. Their reckless jump has left no room for second thoughts or regret. They have to go all the way down, even though they could have avoided it. The same thing happens with the mind. Once it gives in to anger, love, or any other passion, it can't stop itself. Its own weight and the pull of vice will drag the person down and throw him into the depths.

on-anger_book-1.originalText: The best plan is to reject straightway the first incentives to anger, to resist its very beginnings, and to take care not to be betrayed into it: for if once it begins to carry us away, it is hard to get back again into a healthy condition, because reason goes for nothing when once passion has been admitted to the mind, and has by our own free will been given a certain authority, it will for the future do as much as it chooses, not only as much as you will allow it. The enemy, I repeat, must be met and driven back at the outermost frontier-line: for when he has once entered the city and passed its gates, he will not allow his prisoners to set bounds to his victory. The mind does not stand apart and view its passions from without, so as not to permit them to advance further than they ought, but it is itself changed into a passion, and is therefore unable to check what once was useful and wholesome strength, now that it has become degenerate and misapplied: for passion and reason, as I said before, have not distinct and separate provinces, but consist of the changes of the mind itself for better or for worse. How then can reason recover itself when it is conquered and held down by vices, when it has given way to anger? or how can it extricate itself from a confused mixture, the greater part of which consists of the lower qualities?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
The best plan is to reject anger right from the start. Fight it at the very beginning. Don't let yourself get tricked into it. Once anger starts carrying you away, it's hard to get back to normal. Once you let passion into your mind and give it some authority by your own choice, it will do whatever it wants from then on — not just what you're willing to allow.

You have to meet this enemy at the border and drive it back. Once it enters the city and gets past the gates, it won't let its prisoners limit its victory.

Your mind can't stand outside and watch its passions from a distance. It can't say "okay, that's far enough." The mind itself becomes the passion. So it can't stop what used to be useful strength, now that it's become twisted and misused.

Passion and reason don't live in separate areas, as I said before. They're just the mind itself changing for better or worse. So how can reason recover when it's been conquered and held down by bad impulses? How can it escape from a messy mixture where most of it has become something lower?

on-anger_book-1.originalText: "But," argues our adversary, "some men when in anger control themselves." Do they so far control themselves that they do nothing which anger dictates, or some what? If they do nothing thereof, it becomes evident that anger is not essential to the conduct of affairs, although your sect advocated it as possessing greater strength than reason . . . . Finally, I ask, is anger stronger or weaker than reason? If stronger, how can reason impose any check upon it, since it is only the less powerful that obey: if weaker, then reason is competent to effect its ends without anger, and does not need the help of a less powerful quality. "But some angry men remain consistent and control themselves." When do they do so? It is when their anger is disappearing and leaving them of its own accord, not when it was red-hot, for then it was more powerful than they. What then? do not men, even in the height of their anger, sometimes let their enemies go whole and unhurt, and refrain from injuring them? "They do: but when do they do so? It is when one passion overpowers another, and either fear or greed gets the upper hand for a while. On such occasions, it is not thanks to reason that anger is stilled, but owing to an untrustworthy and fleeting truce between the passions.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "But," our opponent argues, "some people control themselves when they're angry." Do they control themselves so well that they do nothing anger tells them to do? Or do they still do some of what anger demands? If they do nothing anger tells them, then clearly we don't need anger to handle our affairs. Your philosophy school claimed anger was stronger than reason, but this proves otherwise. Let me ask you: is anger stronger or weaker than reason? If it's stronger, how can reason stop it? Only weaker things obey stronger ones. If anger is weaker, then reason can do its job without anger's help. It doesn't need assistance from something less powerful. "But some angry people stay consistent and control themselves." When do they do this? Only when their anger is already fading and leaving on its own — not when it was burning hot. When anger was at its peak, it was stronger than they were. So what about this: don't people sometimes spare their enemies even when they're furious? Don't they sometimes hold back from hurting them? "Yes, they do. But when?" Only when one emotion overpowers another. Fear or greed takes control for a moment. In those cases, reason doesn't calm the anger. It's just an unreliable, temporary truce between competing passions.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
In the next place, anger has nothing useful in itself, and does
not rouse up the mind to warlike deeds: for a virtue, being
self-sufficient, never needs the assistance of a vice: whenever it
needs an impetuous effort, it does not become angry, but rises to
the occasion, and excites or soothes itself as far as it deems
requisite, just as the machines which hurl darts may be twisted to
a greater or lesser degree of tension at the manager’s pleasure.
“Anger,” says Aristotle, “is necessary, nor can any fight be won
without it, unless it fills the mind, and kindles up the spirit.
It must, however, be made use of, not as a general, but as a soldier,”
Now this is untrue; for if it listens to reason and follows whither
reason leads, it is no longer anger, whose characteristic is
obstinacy: if, again, it is disobedient and will not be quiet when
ordered, but is carried away by its own wilful and headstrong
spirit, it is then as useless an aid to the mind as a soldier who
disregards the sounding of the retreat would be to a general.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
Let me tackle another point: anger has no use at all. It doesn't prepare the mind for battle. True virtue is complete on its own — it never needs help from a vice. When virtue needs a burst of energy, it doesn't get angry. Instead, it rises to meet the challenge. It stirs itself up or calms itself down as needed, like a catapult that can be wound tighter or looser depending on what the operator wants.

Aristotle says, "Anger is necessary. You can't win any fight without it filling your mind and firing up your spirit. But you should use it like a soldier, not like a general."

This is wrong. If anger listens to reason and goes where reason leads, then it's not really anger anymore. Anger's defining trait is stubbornness. But if anger won't listen and refuses to quiet down when ordered — if it gets carried away by its own reckless, headstrong nature — then it's as useless to the mind as a soldier who ignores the retreat signal would be to his general.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
If,
therefore, anger allows limits to be imposed upon it, it must be
called by some other name, and ceases to be anger, which I understand
to be unbridled and unmanageable: and if it does not allow limits
to be imposed upon it, it is harmful and not to be counted among
aids: wherefore either anger is not anger, or it is useless: for
if any man demands the infliction of punishment, not because he is
eager for the punishment itself, but because it is right to inflict
it, he ought not to be counted as an angry man: that will be the
useful soldier, who knows how to obey orders: the passions cannot
obey any more than they can command.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: So if anger can be controlled and limited, then it's not really anger anymore — it's something else. True anger is wild and uncontrollable. But if anger can't be controlled, then it's harmful and useless. Either way, anger itself doesn't help us. When someone demands punishment not because they want revenge, but because it's the right thing to do, they're not angry — they're acting from principle. That's like a good soldier who follows orders. Emotions can't follow orders any more than they can give them.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
For this cause reason will never call to its aid blind and fierce
impulses, over whom she herself possesses no authority, and which
she never can restrain save by setting against them similar and
equally powerful passions, as for example, fear against anger, anger
against sloth, greed against timidity. May virtue never come to
such a pass, that reason should fly for aid to vices! The mind can
find no safe repose there, it must needs be shaken and tempest-tossed
if it be safe only because of its own defects, if it cannot be brave
without anger, diligent without greed, quiet without fear: such is
the despotism under which a man must live if he becomes the slave
of a passion. Are you not ashamed to put virtues under the patronage
of vices? Then, too, reason ceases to have any power if she can do
nothing without passion, and begins to be equal and like unto
passion; for what difference is there between them if passion without
reason be as rash as reason without passion is helpless? They are
both on the same level, if one cannot exist without the other. Yet
who could endure that passion should be made equal to reason? “Then,”
says our adversary, “passion is useful, provided it be moderate.”
Nay, only if it be useful by nature: but if it be disobedient
to authority and reason, al that we gain by its moderation is that
the less there is of it, the less harm it does: wherefore a moderate
passion is nothing but a moderate evil.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: This is why reason will never call on blind, violent impulses for help. Reason has no power over these impulses and can only control them by setting equally strong passions against them — like using fear to fight anger, or anger to fight laziness, or greed to fight timidity. May virtue never sink so low that reason has to beg vices for help! The mind can't find peace this way. It will always be shaken and storm-tossed if it's only safe because of its own flaws. If you can't be brave without anger, hardworking without greed, or calm without fear — then you're living under tyranny. You've become the slave of passion. Aren't you ashamed to put virtues under the protection of vices? Besides, reason loses all its power if it can't do anything without passion. It becomes equal to passion — no different from it. What's the difference between them if passion without reason is as reckless as reason without passion is helpless? They're both on the same level if one can't exist without the other. Yet who could stand making passion equal to reason? "But," our opponent says, "passion is useful if it's kept moderate." No — only if it's useful by nature. But if passion fights against authority and reason, then all we gain from moderating it is that the less we have, the less harm it does. So a moderate passion is nothing but a moderate evil.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
“But,” argues he, “against our enemies anger is necessary.” In
no case is it less necessary; since our attacks ought not to be
disorderly, but regulated and under control. What, indeed, is it
except anger, so ruinous to itself, that overthrows barbarians, who
have so much more bodily strength than we, and are so much better
able to endure fatigue? Gladiators, too, protect themselves by
skill, but expose themselves to wounds when they are angry. Moreover,
of what use is anger, when the same end can be arrived at by reason?
Do you suppose that a hunter is angry with the beasts he kills? Yet
he meets them when they attack him, and follows them when they flee
from him, all of which is managed by reason without anger. When so
many thousands of Cimbri and Teutones poured over the Alps, what
was it that caused them to perish so completely, that no messenger,
only common rumour, carried the news of that great defeat to their
homes, except that with them anger stood in the place of courage?
and anger, although sometimes it overthrows and breaks to pieces
whatever it meets, yet is more often its own destruction. Who can
be braver than the Germans? who charge more boldly? who have more
love of arms, among which they are born and bred, for which alone
they care, to the neglect of everything else? Who can be more
hardened to undergo every hardship, since a large part of them have
no store of clothing for the body, no shelter from the continual
rigour of the climate: yet Spaniards and Gauls, and even the unwarlike
races of Asia and Syria cut them down before the main legion comes
within sight, nothing but their own irascibility exposing them to
death.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "But," someone argues, "we need anger when fighting our enemies." Actually, that's when we need it least. Our attacks should be organized and controlled, not wild and random. What destroys barbarians — who are stronger than us and can take more punishment — if not anger, which ruins itself? Gladiators protect themselves with skill, but leave themselves open to wounds when they get angry. And what's the point of anger when reason can achieve the same result? Do you think a hunter is angry with the animals he kills? Yet he faces them when they attack and chases them when they run — all managed by reason, not anger. When thousands of Cimbri and Teutones poured over the Alps, what caused them to be destroyed so completely that only rumors — not even a single messenger — brought news of their defeat back home? It was because they used anger instead of courage. And anger, even when it smashes whatever it hits, more often destroys itself. Who could be braver than the Germans? Who charges more boldly? Who loves weapons more — weapons they're born with, raised with, the only thing they care about while ignoring everything else? Who can endure hardship better, when most of them have no clothing for their bodies, no shelter from the endless harsh weather? Yet Spaniards and Gauls, even the unwarlike peoples of Asia and Syria, cut them down before the main Roman legion even comes into sight. Nothing kills them except their own quick temper.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Give but intelligence to those minds, and discipline
to those bodies of theirs, which now are ignorant of vicious
refinements, luxury, and wealth,—to say nothing more, we should
certainly be obliged to go back to the ancient Roman habits of life.
By what did Fabius restore the shattered forces of the state, except
by knowing how to delay and spin out time, which angry men know not
how to do? The empire, which then was at its last gasp, would have
perished if Fabius had been as daring as anger urged him to be: but
he took thought about the condition of affairs, and after counting
his force, no part of which could be lost without everything being
lost with it, he laid aside thoughts of grief and revenge, turning
his sole attention to what was profitable and to making the most
of his opportunities, and conquered his anger before he conquered
Hannibal.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Give these people some wisdom and train their bodies properly — bodies that right now know nothing about harmful luxuries and wealth. If we did that, we would have to return to the old Roman way of life. How did Fabius save Rome when its armies were broken? By knowing how to wait and take his time — something angry men can never do. The empire was dying. It would have collapsed if Fabius had been as reckless as his anger wanted him to be. But he thought carefully about the situation. He counted his forces and knew he couldn't afford to lose any of them without losing everything. So he put aside thoughts of grief and revenge. He focused only on what would help and on making the best use of his chances. He conquered his anger before he conquered Hannibal.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
What did Scipio do? Did he not leave behind Hannibal and
the Carthaginian army, and all with whom he had a right to be angry,
and carry over the war into Africa with such deliberation that he
made his enemies think him luxurious and lazy? What did the second
Scipio do? Did he not remain a long, long time before Numantia, and
bear with calmness the reproach to himself and to his country that
Numantia took longer to conquer than Carthage? By blockading and
investing his enemies, he brought them to such straits that they
perished by their own swords. Anger, therefore, is not useful even
in wars or battles: for it is prone to rashness, and while trying
to bring others into danger, does not guard itself against danger.
The most trustworthy virtue is that which long and carefully considers
itself, controls itself, and slowly and deliberately brings itself
to the front.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: What did Scipio do? He left Hannibal and the Carthaginian army behind — all the people he had good reason to hate. Then he took the war to Africa. He moved so deliberately that his enemies thought he was soft and lazy. What about the second Scipio? He stayed outside Numantia for a very long time. People criticized both him and his country, saying it was taking longer to conquer Numantia than it had taken to conquer Carthage. But he kept his cool. He blockaded his enemies and wore them down until they killed themselves with their own swords. So anger isn't even useful in wars or battles. Anger makes you reckless. While you're trying to put others in danger, you forget to protect yourself. The most reliable strength comes from thinking things through carefully, staying in control, and moving forward slowly and deliberately.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
“What, then,” asks our adversary, “is a good man not to be
angry if he sees his father murdered or his mother outraged?” No,
he will not be angry, but will avenge them, or protect them. Why
do you fear that filial piety will not prove a sufficient spur
to him even without anger? You may as well say—“What then? When a
good man sees his father or his son being cut down, I suppose he
will not weep or faint,” as we see women do whenever any trifling
rumour of danger reaches them. The good man will do his duty without
disturbance or fear, and he will perform the duty of a good man,
so as to do nothing unworthy of a man. My father will be murdered:
then I will defend him: he has been slain, then I will avenge him,
not because I am grieved, but because it is my duty. “Good men are
made angry by injuries done to their friends.” When you say this,
Theophrastus, you seek to throw discredit upon more manly maxims;
you leave the judge and appeal to the mob: because every one is
angry when such things befall his own friends, you suppose that men
will decide that it is their duty to do what they do: for as a rule
every man considers a passion which he recognises to be a righteous
one. But he does the same thing if the hot water is not ready for
his drink, if a glass be broken, or his shoe splashed with mud. It
is not filial piety, but weakness of mind that produces this anger,
as children weep when they lose their parents, just as they do when
they lose their toys.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: "What then?" our opponent asks. "Should a good man not get angry when he sees his father murdered or his mother attacked?" No, he won't be angry. But he will take revenge or protect them. Why do you worry that love for his family won't be enough to motivate him without anger? You might as well ask, "What then? When a good man sees his father or son being killed, I suppose he won't weep or faint?" — like we see women do when they hear even small rumors of danger. The good man will do his duty without getting upset or afraid. He will act like a good man should, doing nothing unworthy of a man. If my father is about to be murdered, I will defend him. If he has been killed, I will avenge him — not because I'm heartbroken, but because it's my duty. "Good men get angry when their friends are wronged." When you say this, Theophrastus, you're trying to discredit stronger principles. You abandon reason and appeal to the crowd. Because everyone gets angry when bad things happen to their friends, you assume people will decide this is what they ought to do. Usually, everyone thinks the emotions they feel are justified. But the same person gets angry if his hot water isn't ready, if a glass breaks, or if his shoe gets muddy. This anger doesn't come from love of family — it comes from weakness of mind. It's like children who cry when they lose their parents the same way they cry when they lose their toys.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
To feel anger on behalf of one’s friends does
not show a loving, but a weak mind: it is admirable and worthy
conduct to stand forth as the defender of one’s parents, children,
friends, and countrymen, at the call of duty itself, acting of one’s
own free will, forming a deliberate judgment, and looking forward
to the future, not in an impulsive, frenzied fashion. No passion
is more eager for revenge than anger, and for that very reason it
is unapt to obtain it: being over hasty and frantic, like almost
all desires, it hinders itself in the attainment of its own object,
and therefore has never been useful either in peace or war: for it
makes peace like war, and when in arms forgets that Mars belongs
to neither side, and falls into the power of the enemy, because
it is not in its own. In the next place, vices ought not to be
received into common use because on some occasions they have effected
somewhat: for so also fevers are good for certain kinds of ill-health,
but nevertheless it is better to be altogether free from them: it
is a hateful mode of cure to owe one’s health to disease. Similarly,
although anger, like poison, or falling headlong, or being shipwrecked,
may have unexpectedly done good, yet it ought not on that account
to be classed as wholesome, for poisons have often proved good for
the health.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
Getting angry on behalf of your friends doesn't show love — it shows weakness. What's truly admirable is defending your parents, children, friends, and countrymen out of duty. Act with purpose, make deliberate choices, and think ahead. Don't act impulsively or wildly.

No emotion craves revenge more than anger. But that's exactly why it fails to get revenge. Anger is too hasty and frantic, like most desires. It gets in its own way and defeats itself. That's why anger has never been useful in peace or war. It turns peace into war, and in battle it forgets that victory can go either way. Anger makes you vulnerable to your enemies because you lose control of yourself.

Besides, we shouldn't accept vices just because they sometimes work. Fevers can help cure certain diseases, but it's still better to never have a fever at all. It's a terrible way to get healthy — owing your health to sickness. The same goes for anger. Sure, like poison or falling off a cliff or getting shipwrecked, anger might accidentally do some good. But that doesn't make it healthy. After all, poison sometimes helps people too.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Moreover, qualities which we ought to possess become better
and more desirable the more extensive they are: if justice is a
good thing, no one will say that it would be better if any part
were subtracted from it; if bravery is a good thing, no one would
wish it to be in any way curtailed: consequently the greater anger
is, the better it is, for who ever objected to a good thing being
increased? But it is not expedient that anger should be increased:
therefore it is not expedient that it should exist at all, for that
which grows bad by increase cannot be a good thing. “Anger is
useful,” says our adversary, “because it makes men more ready to
fight.” According to that mode of reasoning, then, drunkenness also
is a good thing, for it makes men insolent and daring, and many use
their weapons better when the worse for liquor: nay, according to
that reasoning, also, you may call frenzy and madness essential to
strength, because madness often makes men stronger.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Think about it this way: good qualities become better when you have more of them. If justice is good, no one would say we should have less justice. If courage is good, no one wants it weakened. So if anger were truly good, then more anger would always be better. Who complains when something good increases? But we don't want anger to increase — we know that makes things worse. So anger can't be good at all. If something becomes harmful when you get more of it, it was never good to begin with. "But anger is useful," my opponent argues, "because it makes people fight harder." By that logic, being drunk is also good because it makes people bold and reckless. Many people fight better when they're drunk. Following this same reasoning, you might as well say that madness and insanity are essential for strength, since crazy people are often stronger than normal people.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Why, does not
fear often by the rule of contraries make men bolder, and does not
the terror of death rouse up even arrant cowards to join battle?
Yet anger, drunkenness, fear, and the like, are base and temporary
incitements to action, and can furnish no arms to virtue, which has
no need of vices, although they may at times be of some little
assistance to sluggish and cowardly minds. No man becomes
braver through anger, except one who without anger would not have
been brave at all: anger does not therefore come to assist courage,
but to take its place. What are we to say to the argument that, if
anger were a good thing it would attach itself to all the best men?
Yet the most irascible of creatures are infants, old men, and sick
people. Every weakling is naturally prone to complaint.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Sure, fear sometimes makes people bolder through reverse psychology. And the terror of death can push even complete cowards into battle. But anger, drunkenness, fear, and similar emotions are low and temporary ways to motivate action. They can't truly arm virtue, which doesn't need vices to help it — though these emotions might occasionally nudge lazy and cowardly minds into motion. No one becomes braver through anger, except someone who wouldn't be brave at all without it. So anger doesn't assist courage — it replaces it. Here's another point: if anger were actually good, wouldn't it attach itself to all the best people? But the most hot-tempered creatures are babies, old people, and sick people. Every weakling naturally tends toward complaint.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
It is impossible, says Theophrastus, for a good man not to be
angry with bad men. By this reasoning, the better a man is, the
more irascible he will be: yet will he not rather be more tranquil,
more free from passions, and hating no one: indeed, what reason has
he for hating sinners, since it is error that leads them into such
crimes? now it does not become a sensible man to hate the erring,
since if so he will hate himself: let him think how many things he
does contrary to good morals, how much of what he has done stands
in need of pardon, and he will soon become angry with himself also,
for no righteous judge pronounces a different judgment in his own
case and in that of others. No one, I affirm, will be found who can
acquit himself. Every one when he calls himself innocent looks
rather to external witnesses than to his own conscience. How much
more philanthropic it is to deal with the erring in a gentle and
fatherly spirit, and to call them into the right course instead of
hunting them down? When a man is wandering about our fields because
he has lost his way, it is better to place him on the right path
than to drive him away.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Theophrastus says a good man can't help but get angry with bad men. If this were true, then the better a man is, the angrier he would be. But wouldn't he actually be more peaceful, more free from strong emotions, and hate no one? What reason does he have to hate sinners, when it's just their mistakes that lead them to crime? A wise man shouldn't hate people who make errors — if he did, he'd have to hate himself too. Let him think about how many things he does against good morals, how much of what he's done needs forgiveness. Soon he'll be angry with himself as well. No fair judge makes different rules for himself than for others. I promise you — no one can declare themselves completely innocent. When people call themselves innocent, they look to outside witnesses rather than their own conscience. How much kinder it is to treat people who make mistakes with a gentle, fatherly spirit. Call them back to the right path instead of hunting them down. When someone is wandering lost in our fields, it's better to show them the right way than to chase them off.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
The sinner ought, therefore, to be corrected both by warning
and by force, both by gentle and harsh means, and may be made a
better man both towards himself and others by chastisement, but not
by anger: for who is angry with the patient whose wounds he is
tending? “But they cannot be corrected, and there is nothing in
them that is gentle or that admits of good hope.” Then let
them be removed from mortal society, if they are likely to deprave
every one with whom they come in contact, and let them cease to be
bad men in the only way in which they can: yet let this be done
without hatred: for what reason have I for hating the man to whom
I am doing the greatest good, since I am rescuing him from himself?
Does a man hate his own limbs when he cuts them off? That is not
an act of anger, but a lamentable method of healing.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: So when someone does wrong, we should correct them with both warnings and force, both gentle and harsh methods. We can make them better people — both for themselves and others — through punishment, but not through anger. After all, does a doctor get angry at a patient whose wounds he's treating? "But some people can't be corrected. There's nothing gentle in them, nothing that gives us hope." Then remove them from society, if they're going to corrupt everyone they meet. Let them stop being bad in the only way they can. But do this without hatred. Why should I hate someone I'm doing the greatest good for? I'm saving him from himself. Does a man hate his own limbs when he cuts them off? That's not anger — it's a sad but necessary cure.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
We knock mad
dogs on the head, we slaughter fierce and savage bulls, and we doom
scabby sheep to the knife, lest they should infect our flocks: we
destroy monstrous births, and we also drown our children if they
are born weakly or unnaturally formed; to separate what is useless
from what is sound is an act, not of anger, but of reason. Nothing
becomes one who inflicts punishment less than anger, because the
punishment has all the more power to work reformation if the sentence
be pronounced with deliberate judgment. This is why Socrates said
to the slave, “I would strike you, were I not angry.” He put off
the correction of the slave to a calmer season; at the moment, he
corrected himself. Who can boast that he has his passions, under
control, when Socrates did not dare to trust himself to his anger?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: We put down rabid dogs. We slaughter wild bulls. We kill diseased sheep before they infect the flock. We destroy deformed newborns, and we also drown children who are born weak or misshapen. Separating the harmful from the healthy isn't anger — it's reason. Nothing hurts punishment more than anger, because punishment works better when the sentence comes from clear judgment. This is why Socrates told his slave, "I would hit you if I weren't angry." He delayed correcting the slave until he felt calmer. In that moment, he corrected himself instead. Who can claim to control their emotions when even Socrates didn't trust himself with his anger?

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
We do not, therefore, need an angry chastiser to punish the
erring and wicked: for since anger is a crime of the mind, it is
not right that sins should be punished by sin. “What! am I not to
be angry with a robber, or a poisoner?” No: for I am not angry with
myself when I bleed myself. I apply all kinds of punishment as
remedies. You are as yet only in the first stage of error, and do
not go wrong seriously, although you do so often: then I will try
to amend you by a reprimand given first in private and then in
public.[4] You, again, have gone too far to be restored to
virtue by words alone; you must be kept in order by disgrace. For
the next, some stronger measure is required, something that he can
feel must be branded upon him; you, sir, shall be sent into exile
and to a desert place. The next man’s thorough villany needs harsher
remedies: chains and public imprisonment must be applied to him.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: We don't need an angry judge to punish people who do wrong. Since anger is itself a sin of the mind, it's not right to punish sins with sin. "What! Should I not be angry with a thief or a poisoner?" No — I'm not angry with myself when I draw my own blood for medical reasons. I use all kinds of punishments as medicine. You're still in the early stages of error. You don't go seriously wrong, though you mess up often. I'll try to fix you with a scolding — first in private, then in public if needed. You've gone too far to be restored by words alone. You need to be kept in line by public shame. The next person needs something stronger — something he can really feel branded on him. You, sir, will be sent into exile to a desert place. This next man's complete wickedness needs harsher medicine: chains and public prison.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
You, lastly, have an incurably vicious mind, and add crime to crime:
you have come to such a pass, that you are not influenced by the
arguments which are never wanting to recommend evil, but sin itself
is to you a sufficient reason for sinning: you have so steeped your
whole heart in wickedness, that wickedness cannot be taken from you
without bringing your heart with it. Wretched man! you have long
sought to die; we will do you good service, we will take away that
madness from which you suffer, and to you who have so long lived a
misery to yourself and to others, we will give the only good thing
which remains, that is, death. Why should I be angry with a man
just when I am doing him good: sometimes the truest form of compassion
is to put a man to death. If I were a skilled and learned physician,
and were to enter a hospital, or a rich[5] man’s house, I should
not have prescribed the same treatment for all the patients who
were suffering from various diseases. I see different kinds of vice
in the vast number of different minds, and am called in to heal the
whole body of citizens: let us seek for the remedies proper for
each disease.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: You have a mind that's completely corrupt. You pile crime on top of crime. You've reached the point where you don't even need reasons to do evil anymore — sin itself is reason enough for you to sin. You've soaked your whole heart in wickedness so deeply that we can't remove the wickedness without tearing out your heart along with it. You miserable man! You've wanted to die for a long time. We'll do you a favor. We'll take away the madness you suffer from. To you who have been a burden to yourself and everyone else for so long, we'll give the only good thing left: death. Why should I be angry with someone when I'm actually helping him? Sometimes the truest kindness is to kill a person. If I were a skilled doctor entering a hospital or a rich man's house, I wouldn't prescribe the same treatment for every patient suffering from different diseases. I see different kinds of vice in all these different minds. I've been called to heal the whole community of citizens. Let's find the right cure for each disease.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
This man may be cured by his own sense of honour,
that one by travel, that one by pain, that one by want, that one
by the sword. If, therefore, it becomes my duty as a magistrate to
put on black[6] robes, and summon an assembly by the sound of a
trumpet,[7] I shall walk to the seat of judgment not in a rage
or in a hostile spirit, but with the countenance of a judge; I shall
pronounce the formal sentence in a grave and gentle rather than a
furious voice, and shall bid them proceed sternly, yet not
angrily. Even when I command a criminal to be beheaded, when I sew
a parricide up in a sack, when I send a man to be punished by
military law, when I fling a traitor or public enemy down the
Tarpeian Rock, I shall be free from anger, and shall look and feel
just as though I were crushing snakes and other venomous creatures.
“Anger is necessary to enable us to punish.” What? do you think
that the law is angry with men whom it does not know, whom it has
never seen, who it hopes will never exist?
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: One person might be cured by his own sense of honor. Another by travel. Another by pain, poverty, or the sword. So if I have to put on my black robes as a magistrate and call an assembly with a trumpet, I'll walk to the judgment seat calmly — not in rage or with a hostile spirit, but with the face of a judge. I'll pronounce the sentence in a serious and gentle voice, not a furious one. I'll tell them to proceed sternly, but not angrily. Even when I order a criminal beheaded, when I sew a murderer into a sack, when I send someone to military punishment, when I throw a traitor off the Tarpeian Rock — I'll be free from anger. I'll look and feel just like I'm crushing snakes or other poisonous creatures. "But anger is necessary for punishment!" Really? Do you think the law is angry with people it doesn't know, has never seen, and hopes will never exist?

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
We ought, therefore, to
adopt the law’s frame of mind, which does not become angry, but
merely defines offences: for, if it is right for a good man to be
angry at wicked crimes, it will also be right for him to be moved
with envy at the prosperity of wicked men: what, indeed, is more
scandalous than that in some cases the very men, for whose deserts
no fortune could be found bad enough, should flourish and actually
be the spoiled children of success? Yet he will see their affluence
without envy, just as he sees their crimes without anger: a good
judge condemns wrongful acts, but does not hate them. “What then?
when the wise man is dealing with something of this kind, will his
mind not be affected by it and become excited beyond its usual
wont?” I admit that it will: he will experience a slight and trifling
emotion; for, as Zeno says, “Even in the mind of the wise man, a
scar remains after the wound is quite healed.” He will, therefore,
feel certain hints and semblances of passions; but he will be free
from the passions themselves.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: We should think like the law thinks. The law doesn't get angry — it just defines what counts as a crime. If it's right for a good person to get angry at evil acts, then it would also be right for them to feel envious when evil people prosper. And what's more outrageous than seeing the very people who deserve the worst punishment actually thriving and being spoiled by success? Yet a good person will watch their wealth without envy, just as they watch their crimes without anger. A good judge condemns wrong acts but doesn't hate them. "But wait," you might ask, "when a wise person deals with something like this, won't their mind be affected? Won't they get more stirred up than usual?" I'll admit it — yes, they will. They'll feel a slight, minor emotion. As Zeno says, "Even in a wise person's mind, a scar remains after the wound has completely healed." So they will feel certain hints and shadows of emotions. But they'll be free from the emotions themselves.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Aristotle says that “certain passions, if one makes a proper
use of them, act as arms”: which would be true if, like weapons of
war, they could be taken up or laid aside at the pleasure of their
wielder. These arms, which Aristotle assigns to virtue, fight of
their own accord, do not wait to be seized by the hand, and possess
a man instead of being possessed by him. We have no need of
external weapons, nature has equipped us sufficiently by giving us
reason. She has bestowed this weapon upon us, which is strong,
imperishable, and obedient to our will, not uncertain or capable
of being turned against its master. Reason suffices by itself not
merely to take thought for the future, but to manage our affairs:[8]
what, then, can be more foolish than for reason to beg anger for
protection, that is, for what is certain to beg of what is uncertain?
what is trustworthy of what is faithless? what is whole of what is
sick? What, indeed? since reason is far more powerful by itself
even in performing those operations in which the help of anger seems
especially needful: for when reason has decided that a particular
thing should be done, she perseveres in doing it; not being able
to find anything better than herself to exchange with.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Aristotle says that "certain passions, if you use them properly, act like weapons." That would be true if emotions were like real weapons — something you could pick up or put down whenever you wanted. But these "weapons" that Aristotle gives to virtue fight on their own. They don't wait for you to grab them. They possess you instead of being possessed by you. We don't need external weapons. Nature gave us enough equipment when she gave us reason. She gave us this weapon that is strong, lasting, and obedient to our will. It's not unreliable or likely to turn against us. Reason is enough by itself — not just to plan for the future, but to handle our daily business. So what could be more foolish than for reason to beg anger for protection? Why would something certain ask help from something uncertain? Why would something trustworthy depend on something faithless? Why would something healthy rely on something sick? Besides, reason is far more powerful on its own, even in situations where anger seems most necessary. When reason decides something should be done, it sticks with it. It can't find anything better than itself to trade places with.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
She, therefore,
abides by her purpose when it has once been formed; whereas anger
is often overcome by pity: for it possesses no firm strength, but
merely swells like an empty bladder, and makes a violent beginning,
just like the winds which rise from the earth and are caused by
rivers and marshes, which blow furiously without any continuance:
anger begins with a mighty rush, and then falls away, becoming
fatigued too soon: that which but lately thought of nothing but
cruelty and novel forms of torture, is become quite softened and
gentle when the time comes for punishment to be inflicted. Passion
soon cools, whereas reason is always consistent: yet even in cases
where anger has continued to burn, it often happens that although
there may be many who deserve to die, yet after the death of two
or three it ceases to slay. Its first onset is fierce, just as the
teeth of snakes when first roused from their lair are venomous, but
become harmless after repeated bites have exhausted their poison.
Consequently those who are equally guilty are not equally
punished, and often he who has done less is punished more, because
he fell in the way of anger when it was fresher. It is altogether
irregular; at one time it runs into undue excess, at another it
falls short of its duty: for it indulges its own feelings and gives
sentence according to its caprices, will not listen to evidence,
allows the defence no opportunity of being heard, clings to what
it has wrongly assumed, and will not suffer its opinion to be wrested
from it, even when it is a mistaken one.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Justice sticks to her plan once she's made it. But anger often gets overcome by pity. Anger has no real strength — it just puffs up like an empty balloon and makes a violent start. It's like winds that rise from rivers and swamps: they blow hard at first but don't last. Anger begins with a mighty rush, then collapses and gets tired too quickly. What just moments ago was thinking of nothing but cruelty and new kinds of torture suddenly becomes soft and gentle when it's time to actually punish someone. Passion cools off fast. Reason stays consistent. Even when anger keeps burning, it often happens that after killing two or three people (though many deserve to die), it just stops killing. Its first attack is fierce — like snake fangs when they're first disturbed. The fangs are deadly at first, but become harmless after repeated bites drain their poison. So people who are equally guilty don't get punished equally. Often the person who did less gets punished more, just because he crossed anger's path when it was still fresh. Anger is completely unpredictable. Sometimes it goes too far, sometimes it doesn't go far enough. It follows its own feelings and makes decisions based on whims. It won't listen to evidence. It doesn't let the defense speak. It holds onto wrong assumptions and won't let anyone change its mind, even when it's completely mistaken.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Reason gives each side time to plead; moreover, she herself
demands adjournment, that she may have sufficient scope for the
discovery of the truth; whereas anger is in a hurry: reason wishes
to give a just decision; anger wishes its decision to be thought
just: reason looks no further than the matter in hand; anger is
excited by empty matters hovering on the outskirts of the case: it
is irritated by anything approaching to a confident demeanour, a
loud voice, an unrestrained speech, dainty apparel, high-flown
pleading, or popularity with the public. It often condemns a man
because it dislikes his patron; it loves and maintains error even
when truth is staring it in the face. It hates to be proved wrong,
and thinks it more honourable to persevere in a mistaken line of
conduct than to retract it. I remember Gnaeus Piso, a man who was
free from many vices, yet of a perverse disposition, and one who
mistook harshness for consistency. In his anger he ordered a soldier
to be led off to execution because he had returned from furlough
without his comrade, as though he must have murdered him if he could
not show him. When the man asked for time for search, he would not
grant it: the condemned man was brought outside the rampart, and
was just offering his neck to the axe, when suddenly there appeared
his comrade who was thought to be slain.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Reason gives both sides time to make their case. She even asks for delays so she can find the truth. But anger rushes ahead. Reason wants to make the right decision. Anger just wants people to think its decision is right. Reason focuses on the facts at hand. Anger gets worked up over irrelevant details around the edges of the case. It gets irritated by confident behavior, loud voices, bold speech, fancy clothes, dramatic arguments, or popular support. It often condemns someone just because it dislikes their lawyer. It clings to mistakes even when the truth is obvious. It hates being proved wrong and thinks it's more honorable to stick with a bad decision than to admit error. I remember Gnaeus Piso, a man free from many faults but twisted in nature. He confused cruelty with strength. In his anger, he ordered a soldier executed because the man returned from leave without his companion — as if he must have killed him since he couldn't produce him. When the soldier begged for time to search, Piso refused.
