The condemned man was dragged outside the camp and was about to put his neck to the axe when suddenly his companion appeared — the one everyone thought was dead.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Hereupon the centurion in
charge of the execution bade the guardsman sheathe his sword, and
led the condemned man back to Piso, to restore to him the
innocence which Fortune had restored to the soldier. They were led
into his presence by their fellow soldiers amid the great joy of
the whole camp, embracing one another and accompanied by a vast
crowd. Piso mounted the tribunal in a fury and ordered them both
to be executed, both him who had not murdered and him who had not
been slain. What could be more unworthy than this? Because one was
proved to be innocent, two perished. Piso even added a third: for
he actually ordered the centurion, who had brought back the condemned
man, to be put to death. Three men were set up to die in the same
place because one was innocent. O, how clever is anger at inventing
reasons for its frenzy! “You,” it says, “I order to be executed,
because you have been condemned to death: you, because you have
been the cause of your comrade’s condemnation, and you, because
when ordered to put him to death you disobeyed your general.” He
discovered the means of charging them with three crimes, because
he could find no crime in them.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: So the centurion in charge of the execution told the guard to put away his sword. He led the condemned man back to Piso to restore his innocence — just as Fortune had restored the soldier's life. The soldiers brought both men before Piso. The whole camp rejoiced. They embraced each other, surrounded by a huge crowd. Piso climbed up to his judgment seat in a rage and ordered both men executed — the one who hadn't murdered and the one who hadn't been killed. What could be more outrageous? Because one man was proven innocent, two had to die. Piso even added a third victim. He ordered the centurion who brought back the condemned man to be executed too. Three men were sentenced to die in the same spot because one was innocent. Oh, how clever anger is at finding reasons for its madness! "You," it says, "I order executed because you were condemned to death. You, because you caused your friend's condemnation. And you, because you disobeyed your general when ordered to kill him." He found a way to charge them with three crimes because he couldn't find any real crime in them.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Irascibility, I say, has this fault—it is loth to be ruled:
it is angry with the truth itself, if it comes to light against its
will: it assails those whom it has marked for its victims with
shouting and riotous noise and gesticulation of the entire body,
together with reproaches and curses. Not thus does reason act: but
if it must be so, she silently and quietly wipes out whole households,
destroys entire families of the enemies of the state, together with
their wives and children, throws down their very dwellings, levels
them with the ground, and roots out the names of those who are the
foes of liberty. This she does without grinding her teeth or shaking
her head, or doing anything unbecoming to a judge, whose countenance
ought to be especially calm and composed at the time when he is
pronouncing an important sentence. “What need is there,” asks
Hieronymus, “for you to bite your own lips when you want to strike
some one?” What would he have said, had he seen a proconsul
leap down from the tribunal, snatch the fasces from the lictor, and
tear his own clothes because those of others were not torn as fast
as he wished. Why need you upset the table, throw down the drinking
cups, knock yourself against the columns, tear your hair, smite
your thigh and your breast? How vehement do you suppose anger to
be, if it thus turns back upon itself, because it cannot find vent
on another as fast as it wishes? Such men, therefore, are held back
by the bystanders and are begged to become reconciled with themselves.
But he who while free from anger assigns to each man the penalty
which he deserves, does none of these things.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Anger, I'm telling you, has a major flaw — it hates being controlled. It gets furious at the truth itself when it comes out against its wishes. It attacks its victims with shouting, wild noise, and wild gestures of the whole body, along with insults and curses. Reason doesn't act this way. When reason must destroy, it quietly and calmly wipes out entire households. It destroys whole families of enemies of the state, along with their wives and children. It tears down their homes, levels them to the ground, and erases the names of those who are enemies of freedom. It does this without grinding its teeth or shaking its head, or doing anything unfit for a judge. A judge's face should be especially calm and composed when pronouncing an important sentence. "Why do you need to bite your own lips when you want to hit someone?" asks Hieronymus. What would he have said if he had seen a governor leap down from his platform, grab the ceremonial rods from his attendant, and tear his own clothes because others weren't being torn fast enough for his liking? Why do you need to overturn the table, throw down the cups, bang yourself against the columns, tear your hair, and beat your thigh and chest? How violent do you think anger must be if it turns back on itself this way, just because it can't strike out at others as fast as it wants? People like this have to be held back by bystanders and begged to make peace with themselves. But someone who assigns each person the punishment they deserve while free from anger — he does none of these things.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
He often lets a man
go after detecting his crime, if his penitence for what he has done
gives good hope for the future, if he perceives that the man’s
wickedness is not deeply rooted in his mind, but is only, as the
saying is, skin-deep. He will grant impunity in cases where it will
hurt neither the receiver nor the giver. In some cases he will
punish great crimes more leniently than lesser ones, if the former
were the result of momentary impulse, not of cruelty, while the
latter were instinct with secret, underhand, long-practised craftiness.
The same fault, committed by two separate men, will not be visited
by him with the same penalty, if the one was guilty of it through
carelessness, the other with a premeditated intention of doing
mischief.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: He often lets a person go free even after catching them in a crime. He does this if their regret seems genuine and suggests they'll do better in the future. He looks to see if their bad behavior runs deep or is just surface-level, as people say. He'll grant mercy when it won't harm either the criminal or society. Sometimes he'll punish major crimes more gently than minor ones. This happens when the big crime was a moment of poor judgment rather than cruelty, while the small crime showed hidden, sneaky, long-practiced deception. When two different people commit the same wrong, he won't give them the same punishment. One might have acted carelessly, while the other planned to cause harm.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
In all dealing with crime he will remember that the one
form of punishment is meant to make bad men better, and the other
to put them out of the way. In either case he will look to the
future, not to the past: for, as Plato says, “no wise man punishes
any one because he has sinned, but that he may sin no more: for
what is past cannot be recalled, but what is to come may be checked.”
Those, too, whom he wishes to make examples of the ill success of
wickedness, he executes publicly, not merely in order that they
themselves may die, but that by dying they may deter others
from doing likewise. You see how free from any mental disturbance
a man ought to be who has to weigh and consider all this, when he
deals with a matter which ought to be handled with the utmost care,
I mean, the power of life and death. The sword of justice is
ill-placed in the hands of an angry man.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: When dealing with criminals, he will remember that punishment has two purposes: to reform bad people or to remove them permanently. Either way, he focuses on the future, not the past. As Plato said, "No wise person punishes someone because they sinned, but so they won't sin again. The past cannot be undone, but the future can be changed." When he makes public examples of criminals to show that wickedness doesn't pay, he executes them not just to end their lives, but so their deaths will stop others from following the same path. You can see how calm and clearheaded someone must be to weigh all these factors when handling the ultimate responsibility — the power over life and death. Justice wielded by an angry person is dangerous.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
Neither ought it to be believed that anger contributes anything
to magnanimity: what it gives is not magnanimity but vain glory.
The increase which disease produces in bodies swollen with morbid
humours is not healthy growth, but bloated corpulence. All those
whose madness raises them above human considerations, believe
themselves to be inspired with high and sublime ideas; but there
is no solid ground beneath, and what is built without foundation
is liable to collapse in ruin. Anger has no ground to stand upon,
and does not rise from a firm and enduring foundation, but is a
windy, empty quality, as far removed from true magnanimity as
fool-hardiness from courage, boastfulness from confidence, gloom
from austerity, cruelty from strictness. There is, I say, a great
difference between a lofty and a proud mind: anger brings about
nothing grand or beautiful. On the other hand, to be constantly
irritated seems to me to be the part of a languid and unhappy mind,
conscious of its own feebleness, like folk with diseased bodies
covered with sores, who cry out at the lightest touch. Anger,
therefore, is a vice which for the most part affects women and
children. “Yet it affects men also.” Because many men, too, have
womanish or childish intellects. “But what are we to say? do not
some words fall from angry men which appear to flow from a great
mind?” Yes, to those who know not what true greatness is: as, for
example, that foul and hateful saying, “Let them hate me, provided
they fear me,” which you may be sure was written in Sulla’s time.
I know not which was the worse of the two things he wished
for, that he might be hated or that he might be feared.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: Don't believe that anger makes you brave or noble. What it gives you isn't true courage — it's just empty pride. When disease makes a body swell up with bad fluids, that's not healthy growth. It's just bloating. People who go crazy and think they're above everyone else believe they have deep, inspiring thoughts. But there's nothing solid underneath. What you build without a foundation will collapse. Anger has no foundation either. It doesn't come from anything firm or lasting. It's just windy and empty — as different from true courage as recklessness is from bravery, or bragging is from real confidence, or cruelty is from being strict. There's a huge difference between a noble mind and an arrogant one. Anger never creates anything great or beautiful. Being constantly irritated seems like the mark of a weak, miserable mind that knows it's feeble. It's like people with diseased, sore-covered bodies who scream at the slightest touch. Anger mostly affects women and children. "But it affects men too." Yes, because many men have the minds of women or children. "But what about this — don't angry men sometimes say things that seem to come from greatness?" Sure, they do — but only to people who don't know what real greatness looks like. Take that disgusting, hateful saying: "Let them hate me, as long as they fear me." You can bet that was written in Sulla's time. I don't know which was worse — that he wanted to be hated or that he wanted to be feared.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
It occurs
to his mind that some day people will curse him, plot against him,
crush him: what prayer does he add to this? May all the gods curse
him—for discovering a cure for hate so worthy of it. “Let them
hate.” How? “Provided they obey me?” No! “Provided they approve of
me?” No! How then? “Provided they fear me!” I would not even be
loved upon such terms. Do you imagine that this was a very spirited
saying? You are wrong: this is not greatness, but monstrosity. You
should not believe the words of angry men, whose speech is very
loud and menacing, while their mind within them is as timid as
possible: nor need you suppose that the most eloquent of men, Titus
Livius, was right in describing somebody as being “of a great rather
than a good disposition.” The things cannot be separated: he must
either be good or else he cannot be great, because I take greatness
of mind to mean that it is unshaken, sound throughout, firm and
uniform to its very foundation; such as cannot exist in evil
dispositions. Such dispositions may be terrible, frantic, and
destructive, but cannot possess greatness; because greatness rests
upon goodness, and owes its strength to it. “Yet by speech, action,
and all outward show they will make one think them great.” True,
they will say something which you may think shows a great spirit,
like Gaius Caesar, who when angry with heaven because it interfered
with his ballet-dancers, whom he imitated more carefully than he
attended to them when they acted, and because it frightened his
revels by its thunders, surely ill-directed,[9] challenged Jove to
fight, and that to the death, shouting the Homeric verse:—
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: He realizes that someday people will curse him, plot against him, and destroy him. What prayer does he add to this? May all the gods curse him — for finding a cure for hate so worthy of hatred. "Let them hate." How? "As long as they obey me?" No! "As long as they approve of me?" No! How then? "As long as they fear me!" I wouldn't even want to be loved on those terms. Do you think this was a brave saying? You're wrong. This isn't greatness — it's monstrous. You shouldn't believe the words of angry men. Their speech is loud and threatening, but their minds are as cowardly as possible. And don't suppose that even the most eloquent writer, Titus Livius, was right when he described someone as having "a great rather than a good character." These things can't be separated. A person must either be good or he can't be great. True greatness of mind means it stays unshaken, sound all through, firm and consistent to its very core. This can't exist in evil people. Evil people may be terrible, frantic, and destructive, but they can't have greatness. Greatness rests on goodness and gets its strength from it. "But through their words, actions, and outward show, they'll make you think they're great." True, they'll say something that might seem to show a great spirit — like Gaius Caesar. When he got angry at heaven for interfering with his ballet dancers (whom he copied more carefully than he watched when they performed), and because thunder frightened his parties with poorly aimed noise, he challenged Jupiter to a fight to the death, shouting Homer's verse:

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
“Carry me off, or I will carry thee!”

How great was his madness! He must have believed either that
he could not be hurt even by Jupiter himself, or that he could hurt
even Jupiter itself. I imagine that this saying of his had no small
weight in nerving the minds of the conspirators for their task: for
it seemed to be the height of endurance to bear one who could not
bear Jupiter.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish:
"Take me away, or I'll take you away!"

How insane was that! He must have believed either that not even Jupiter could hurt him, or that he could hurt Jupiter himself. I think this saying of his really motivated the conspirators. It seemed like the ultimate test of patience — having to put up with someone who wouldn't even put up with Jupiter.

on-anger_book-1.originalText:
There is therefore nothing great or noble in anger, even when
it seems to be powerful and to contemn both gods and men alike. Any
one who thinks that anger produces greatness of mind, would think
that luxury produces it: such a man wishes to rest on ivory, to be
clothed with purple, and roofed with gold; to remove lands, embank
seas, hasten the course of rivers, suspend woods in the air. He
would think that avarice shows greatness of mind: for the avaricious
man broods over heaps of gold and silver, treats whole provinces
as merely fields on his estate, and has larger tracts of country
under the charge of single bailiffs than those which consuls once
drew lots to administer. He would think that lust shows greatness
of mind: for the lustful man swims across straits, castrates troops
of boys, and puts himself within reach of the swords of injured
husbands with complete scorn of death. Ambition, too, he would think
shows greatness of mind: for the ambitious man is not content with
office once a year, but, if possible, would fill the calendar of
dignities with his name alone, and cover the whole world with his
titles. It matters nothing to what heights or lengths these passions
may proceed: they are narrow, pitiable, grovelling. Virtue alone
is lofty and sublime, nor is anything great which is not at the
same time tranquil.
on-anger_book-1.plainEnglish: There is nothing great or noble about anger, even when it seems powerful and looks down on both gods and men. Anyone who thinks anger creates greatness of mind might as well think luxury does too. Such a person wants to rest on ivory beds, wear purple clothes, and live under golden roofs. He wants to move mountains, dam up seas, change the course of rivers, and hang forests in mid-air. He would think greed shows greatness of mind too. The greedy man hoards piles of gold and silver. He treats entire provinces like fields on his personal estate. He puts more land under single managers than whole territories that consuls once governed. He would think lust shows greatness of mind as well. The lustful man swims across dangerous waters, castrates groups of boys, and puts himself within reach of angry husbands' swords — completely ignoring the risk of death. He would think ambition shows greatness of mind too. The ambitious man won't settle for holding office once a year. If he could, he would fill the entire calendar with his name alone and cover the whole world with his titles. It doesn't matter how far or high these passions reach — they are narrow, pitiful, and base. Only virtue is lofty and sublime. Nothing is truly great unless it is also peaceful.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: My first book, Novatus, had a more abundant subject: for carriages roll easily down hill:[1] now we must proceed to drier matters. The question before us is whether anger arises from deliberate choice or from impulse, that is, whether it acts of its own accord or like the greater part of those passions which spring up within us without our knowledge. It is necessary for our debate to stoop to the consideration of these matters, in order that it may afterwards be able to rise to loftier themes; for likewise in our bodies the parts which are first set in order are the bones, sinews, and joints, which are by no means fair to see, albeit they are the foundation of our frame and essential to its life: next to them come the parts of which all beauty of face and appearance consists; and after these, colour, which above all else charms the eye, is applied last of all, when the rest of the body is complete.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: My first book, Novatus, had an easier topic to work with. It's like rolling a cart downhill — much simpler. Now we have to tackle drier, harder material. The question before us is this: does anger come from deliberate choice, or from impulse? In other words, does it act on its own, or is it like most other emotions that spring up inside us without our knowledge? We need to work through these basic matters first, so we can rise to higher themes later. Think of it like building a body. First you set the bones, tendons, and joints in place. They're not pretty to look at, but they're the foundation that keeps everything alive. Next come the parts that create all the beauty of face and appearance. Finally, you add color — the thing that charms the eye most of all — but only after the rest of the body is complete.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: There is no doubt that anger is roused by the appearance of an injury being done: but the question before us is, whether anger straightway follows the appearance, and springs up without assistance from the mind, or whether it is roused with the sympathy of the mind. Our (the Stoics') opinion is, that anger can venture upon nothing by itself, without the approval of mind: for to conceive the idea of a wrong having been done, to long to avenge it, and to join the two propositions, that we ought not to have been injured and that it is our duty to avenge our injuries, cannot belong to a mere impulse which is excited without our consent. That impulse is a simple act; this is a complex one, and composed of several parts. The man understands something to have happened: he becomes indignant thereat: he condemns the deed; and he avenges it. All these things cannot be done without his mind agreeing to those matters which touched him.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
There's no doubt that anger is triggered when we think someone has wronged us. But here's the question: Does anger follow immediately from that impression, springing up without any help from our thinking mind? Or does anger need our mind's agreement to get started?

We Stoics believe that anger can't do anything by itself without the mind's approval. Think about it: recognizing that a wrong has been done, wanting revenge, and connecting these two ideas — 'I shouldn't have been hurt' and 'I must get payback' — these can't come from a simple impulse that happens without our consent. A basic impulse is simple. But this anger process is complex, made up of several parts.

Here's what happens: A person notices something has occurred. He gets indignant about it. He judges the action as wrong. Then he seeks revenge. All of these steps can't happen without his mind agreeing to the thoughts that affected him.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Whither, say you, does this inquiry tend? That we may know what anger is: for if it springs up against our will, it never will yield to reason: because all the motions which take place without our volition are beyond our control and unavoidable, such as shivering when cold water is poured over us, or shrinking when we are touched in certain places. Men's hair rises up at bad news, their faces blush at indecent words, and they are seized with dizziness when looking down a precipice; and as it is not in our power to prevent any of these things, no reasoning can prevent their taking place. But anger can be put to flight by wise maxims; for it is a voluntary defect of the mind, and not one of those things which are evolved by the conditions of human life, and which, therefore, may happen even to the wisest of us.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Where is this going, you ask? We need to understand what anger really is. If anger happens against our will, then reason will never defeat it. All movements that happen without our choice are beyond our control and unavoidable. We shiver when cold water hits us. We flinch when touched in sensitive spots. Our hair stands up at bad news. Our faces turn red at crude words. We get dizzy looking down a cliff. Since we can't prevent any of these things, no amount of reasoning will stop them. But anger can be driven away by wisdom. It's a voluntary flaw of the mind — not one of those things that just comes with being human and can happen even to the wisest people.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Among these and in the first place must be ranked that thrill of the mind which seizes us at the thought of wrongdoing. We feel this even when witnessing the mimic scenes of the stage, or when reading about things that happened long ago. We often feel angry with Clodius for banishing Cicero, and with Antonius for murdering him. Who is not indignant with the wars of Marius, the proscriptions of Sulla? who is not enraged against Theodotus and Achillas and the boy king who dared to commit a more than boyish crime?[2] Sometimes songs excite us, and quickened rhythm and the martial noise of trumpets; so, too, shocking pictures and the dreadful sight of tortures, however well deserved, affect our minds. Hence it is that we smile when others are smiling, that a crowd of mourners makes us sad, and that we take a glowing interest in another's battles; all of which feelings are not anger, any more than that which clouds our brow at the sight of a stage shipwreck is sadness, or what we feel, when we read how Hannibal after Cannae beset the walls of Rome, can be called fear. All these are emotions of minds which are loth to be moved, and are not passions, but rudiments which may grow into passions. So, too, a soldier starts at the sound of a trumpet, although he may be dressed as a civilian and in the midst of a profound peace, and camp horses prick up their ears at the clash of arms. It is said that Alexander, when Xenophantus was singing, laid his hand upon his weapons.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: First on our list is that mental thrill we get when we think about wrongdoing. We feel this even when watching plays or reading about ancient history. We often get angry at Clodius for exiling Cicero, and at Antonius for killing him. Who isn't outraged by Marius's wars or Sulla's death lists? Who doesn't rage against Theodotus and Achillas and that boy king who committed such an adult crime? Sometimes songs stir us up, along with fast rhythms and the martial sound of trumpets. Disturbing pictures and terrible scenes of torture affect our minds too, even when the punishment is deserved. This is why we smile when others smile, why a crowd of mourners makes us sad, and why we get fired up about someone else's battles. None of these feelings are actually anger — any more than the frown we get watching a stage shipwreck is real sadness, or what we feel reading about Hannibal threatening Rome after Cannae is real fear. These are just stirrings in minds that don't want to be moved. They're not full passions, but seeds that could grow into passions. A soldier jumps at a trumpet's sound even when he's in civilian clothes during peacetime. War horses perk up their ears at the clash of weapons. They say Alexander reached for his sword when Xenophantus was singing.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
None of these things which casually influence the mind deserve
to be called passions: the mind, if I may so express it, rather
suffers passions to act upon itself than forms them. A passion,
therefore, consists not in being affected by the sights which are
presented to us, but in giving way to our feelings and following
up these chance promptings: for whoever imagines that paleness,
bursting into tears, lustful feelings, deep sighs, sudden flashes
of the eyes, and so forth, are signs of passion and betray the
state of the mind, is mistaken, and does not understand that these
are merely impulses of the body. Consequently, the bravest of men
often turns pale while he is putting on his armour; when the signal
for battle is given, the knees of the boldest soldier shake for a
moment; the heart even of a great general leaps into his mouth just
before the lines clash together, and the hands and feet even of the
most eloquent orator grow stiff and cold while he is preparing to
begin his speech.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: None of these things that randomly affect our minds should be called true emotions. The mind doesn't create these feelings — it just lets them happen to it. Real passion isn't about being affected by what we see around us. It's about giving in to those feelings and chasing after these random impulses. If you think that turning pale, bursting into tears, feeling lust, sighing deeply, or having your eyes flash with anger are signs of real passion that show what's in your mind, you're wrong. You don't understand that these are just bodily reactions. That's why the bravest man often turns pale while putting on his armor. When the battle signal sounds, even the boldest soldier's knees shake for a moment. Even a great general's heart jumps into his throat just before the armies clash. Even the most eloquent speaker's hands and feet go stiff and cold while preparing to give a speech.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Anger must not merely move, but break out of
bounds, being an impulse: now, no impulse can take place without
the consent of the mind: for it cannot be that we should deal with
revenge and punishment without the mind being cognisant of them. A
man may think himself injured, may wish to avenge his wrongs, and
then may be persuaded by some reason or other to give up his intention
and calm down: I do not call that anger, it is an emotion of the
mind which is under the control of reason. Anger is that which goes
beyond reason and carries her away with it: wherefore the first
confusion of a man’s mind when struck by what seems an injury is
no more anger than the apparent injury itself: it is the subsequent
mad rush, which not only receives the impression of the apparent
injury, but acts upon it as true, that is anger, being an exciting
of the mind to revenge, which proceeds from choice and deliberate
resolve. There never has been any doubt that fear produces flight,
and anger a rush forward; consider, therefore, whether you suppose
that anything can be either sought or avoided without the participation
of the mind.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Anger doesn't just move you — it breaks all boundaries. It's an impulse. And no impulse can happen without your mind's consent. You can't deal with revenge and punishment without your mind knowing about it. A man might think someone has wronged him. He might want revenge. Then some reason convinces him to give up the idea and calm down. I don't call that anger. That's just an emotion controlled by reason. Anger is what goes beyond reason and drags reason along with it. So when your mind first gets confused after what seems like an injury — that's not anger any more than the apparent injury itself is. It's the crazy rush that comes next that is anger. This rush not only receives the impression of the apparent injury, but treats it as real and acts on it. Anger is the mind getting excited about revenge through choice and deliberate decision. No one has ever doubted that fear makes us run away, and anger makes us rush forward. So think about this: do you believe anything can be either pursued or avoided without your mind taking part?

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Furthermore, that you may know in what manner passions begin
and swell and gain spirit, learn that the first emotion is involuntary,
and is, as it were, a preparation for a passion, and a threatening
of one. The next is combined with a wish, though not an obstinate
one, as, for example, “It is my duty to avenge myself, because I
have been injured,” or “It is right that this man should be
punished, because he has committed a crime.” The third emotion is
already beyond our control, because it overrides reason, and wishes
to avenge itself, not if it be its duty, but whether or no. We are
not able by means of reason to escape from that first impression
on the mind, any more than we can escape from those things which
we have mentioned as occurring to the body: we cannot prevent other
people’s yawns temping us to yawn:[3] we cannot help winking when
fingers are suddenly darted at our eyes. Reason is unable to overcome
these habits, which perhaps might be weakened by practice and
constant watchfulness: they differ from an emotion which is brought
into existence and brought to an end by a deliberate mental act.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: So you can understand how emotions start and build up and take over, let me explain how it works. The first stage is involuntary — it's like your mind getting ready for an emotion, or being threatened by one. The second stage includes wanting something, though not stubbornly yet. For example: "I should get revenge because someone hurt me," or "This person deserves punishment because they committed a crime." The third stage is already out of our control. It overpowers reason and wants revenge no matter what — not because it's right, but just because. We can't use reason to escape that first mental reaction, any more than we can escape certain physical reactions. We can't stop ourselves from yawning when others yawn. We can't help blinking when fingers suddenly dart toward our eyes. Reason can't overcome these habits. Maybe practice and constant attention could weaken them. But they're different from emotions, which we create and end through deliberate mental choices.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: We must also enquire whether those whose cruelty knows no bounds, and who delight in shedding human blood, are angry when they kill people from whom they have received no injury, and who they themselves do not think have done them any injury; such as were Apollodorus or Phalaris. This is not anger, it is ferocity: for it does not do hurt because it has received injury: but is even willing to receive injury, provided it may do hurt. It does not long to inflict stripes and mangle bodies to avenge its wrongs, but for its own pleasure. What then are we to say? This evil takes its rise from anger; for anger, after it has by long use and indulgence made a man forget mercy, and driven all feelings of human fellowship from his mind, passes finally into cruelty. Such men therefore laugh, rejoice, enjoy themselves greatly, and are as unlike as possible in countenance to angry men, since cruelty is their relaxation.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: We should also ask about people whose cruelty has no limits. They love spilling human blood. Are they angry when they kill people who never hurt them — people they don't even think wronged them? Take men like Apollodorus or Phalaris. This isn't anger anymore. It's savagery. They don't hurt people because they were hurt first. They're willing to be hurt themselves if it means they get to hurt others. They don't want to beat and torture bodies for revenge. They do it for fun. So what's happening here? This evil grows out of anger. When anger gets fed and pampered for a long time, it makes a person forget mercy. It drives out all sense of human connection. Finally, it becomes cruelty. These men laugh and have a good time. They enjoy themselves immensely. They look nothing like angry people — because cruelty has become their entertainment.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: It is said that when Hannibal saw a trench full of human blood, he exclaimed, "O, what a beauteous sight!" How much more beautiful would he have thought it, if it had filled a river or a lake? Why should we wonder that you should be charmed with this sight above all others, you who were born in bloodshed and brought up amid slaughter from a child? Fortune will follow you and favour your cruelty for twenty years, and will display to you everywhere the sight that you love. You will behold it both at Trasumene and at Cannae, and lastly at your own city of Carthage. Volesus, who not long ago, under the Emperor Augustus, was proconsul of Asia Minor, after he had one day beheaded three hundred persons, strutted out among the corpses with a haughty air, as though he had performed some grand and notable exploit, and exclaimed in Greek, "What a kingly action!" What would this man have done, had he been really a king? This was not anger, but a greater and an incurable disease.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: They say that when Hannibal saw a ditch full of human blood, he cried out, "What a beautiful sight!" How much more beautiful would he have thought it if it had filled a river or a lake? Why should we be surprised that you find this sight more charming than any other? You were born in bloodshed and raised among slaughter from childhood. Fortune will follow you and favor your cruelty for twenty years. It will show you everywhere the sight you love. You will see it at Trasimene and at Cannae, and finally at your own city of Carthage. Volesus, who not long ago served as governor of Asia Minor under Emperor Augustus, beheaded three hundred people in one day. Then he strutted around among the corpses with a proud look, as if he had done something grand and remarkable. He shouted in Greek, "What a kingly deed!" What would this man have done if he had actually been a king? This was not anger, but something worse and incurable.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“Virtue,” argues our adversary, “ought to be angry with what
is base, just as she approves of what is honourable.” What should
we think if he said that virtue ought to be both mean and great;
yet this is what he means, when he wants her to be raised and
lowered, because joy at a good action is grand and glorious, while
anger at another’s sin is base and befits a narrow mind: and virtue
will never be guilty of imitating vice while she is repressing it;
she considers anger to deserve punishment for itself, since it often
is even more criminal than the faults which which it is angry. To
rejoice and be glad is the proper and natural function of virtue:
it is as much beneath her dignity to be angry, as to mourn: now,
sorrow is the companion of anger, and all anger ends in sorrow,
either from remorse or from failure. Secondly, if it be the part
of the wise man to be angry with sins, he will be more angry the
greater they are, and will often be angry: from which it follows
that the wise man will not only be angry but irascible. Yet
if we do not believe that great and frequent anger can find any
place in the wise man’s mind, why should we not set him altogether
free from this passion? for there can be no limit, if he ought to
be angry in proportion to what every man does: because he will
either be unjust if he is equally angry at unequal crimes, or he
will be the most irascible of men, if he blazes into wrath as often
as crimes deserve his anger.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Our opponent argues, "Virtue should be angry at what is base, just as she approves of what is honorable." What would we think if he said virtue should be both mean and great? Yet that's exactly what he means when he wants her to be raised and lowered. Joy at a good action is grand and glorious, while anger at another's sin is base and fits a narrow mind. Virtue will never imitate vice while trying to stop it. She considers anger itself deserving of punishment, since it is often even more criminal than the faults it gets angry about. To rejoice and be glad is virtue's proper and natural job. It is beneath her dignity to be angry, just as it is to mourn. Sorrow is anger's companion, and all anger ends in sorrow — either from regret or from failure. Second, if it's the wise man's job to be angry at sins, he will be angrier the greater they are, and will often be angry. This means the wise man will not only be angry but quick to anger. But if we don't believe that great and frequent anger can find any place in the wise man's mind, why shouldn't we free him from this passion entirely? There can be no limit if he ought to be angry in proportion to what every man does. He will either be unjust if he is equally angry at unequal crimes, or he will be the most quick-tempered of men if he blazes into wrath as often as crimes deserve his anger.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
What, too, can be more unworthy of the wise man, than that his
passions should depend upon the wickedness of others? If so, the
great Socrates will no longer be able to return home with the same
expression of countenance with which he set out. Moreover, if it
be the duty of the wise man to be angry at base deeds, and to be
excited and saddened at crimes, then is there nothing more unhappy
than the wise man, for all his life will be spent in anger and
grief. What moment will there be at which he will not see something
deserving of blame? whenever he leaves his house, he will be obliged
to walk among men who are criminals, misers, spendthrifts, profligates,
and who are happy in being so: he can turn his eyes in no direction
without their finding something to shock them. He will faint, if
he demands anger from himself as often as reason calls for it. All
these thousands who are hurrying to the law courts at break of day,
how base are their causes, and how much baser their advocates? One
impugns his father’s will, when he would have done better to deserve
it; another appears as the accuser of his mother; a third comes to
inform against a man for committing the very crime of which he
himself is yet more notoriously guilty. The judge, too, is chosen
to condemn men for doing what he himself has done, and the audience
takes the wrong side, led astray by the fine voice of the pleader.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
What could be more unworthy of a wise person than letting their emotions depend on how wicked other people are? If that were true, then even the great Socrates couldn't come home with the same calm expression he had when he left.

Besides, if it's the wise person's job to get angry at evil deeds and feel upset about crimes, then no one would be more miserable than the wise person. His whole life would be spent in anger and grief. When would he have a moment without seeing something worth condemning? Every time he leaves his house, he'd have to walk among criminals, misers, wastrels, and degenerates — and people who are proud to be that way. He couldn't look anywhere without seeing something that would shock him. He'd collapse from exhaustion if he got angry every time reason demanded it.

Look at all those thousands rushing to the courts at dawn. How shameful their cases are, and how much more shameful their lawyers! One person attacks his father's will when he should have tried to deserve it instead. Another accuses his own mother. A third comes to inform on someone for the very crime he himself is even more obviously guilty of. The judge is chosen to condemn people for doing what he himself has done. And the audience takes the wrong side, fooled by the smooth voice of some speaker.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Why need I dwell upon individual cases? Be assured, when you
see the Forum crowded with a multitude, the Saepta[4] swarming
with people, or the great Circus, in which the greater part of the
people find room to show themselves at once, that among them there
are as many vices as there are men. Among those whom you see in the
garb of peace there is no peace: for a small profit any one of them
will attempt the ruin of another: no one can gain anything save by
another’s loss. They hate the fortunate and despise the unfortunate:
they grudgingly endure the great, and oppress the small: they are
fired by divers lusts: they would wreck everything for the sake of
a little pleasure or plunder: they live as though they were in a
school of gladiators, fighting with the same people with whom they
live: it is like a society of wild beasts, save that beasts are
tame with one another, and refrain from biting their own species,
whereas men tear one another, and gorge themselves upon one another.
They differ from dumb animals in this alone, that the latter are
tame with those who feed them, whereas the rage of the former preys
on those very persons by whom they were brought up.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Why should I give you specific examples? Just look around. When you see the Forum packed with crowds, the voting grounds swarming with people, or the great Circus where most of the population gathers at once — know this: there are as many vices as there are people. Among those you see dressed in peaceful clothes, there is no peace. For a small profit, any one of them will try to destroy another. No one can gain anything without someone else losing. They hate successful people and look down on the unfortunate. They barely tolerate the powerful while crushing the weak. They burn with different desires. They would wreck everything for a bit of pleasure or profit. They live like gladiators in training — fighting the same people they live with every day. It's like a society of wild animals, except animals are gentle with their own kind and don't bite members of their own species. But humans tear each other apart and devour one another. They differ from dumb animals in only this way: animals are tame with those who feed them, but human rage attacks the very people who raised them.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: The wise man will never cease to be angry, if he once begins, so full is every place of vices and crimes. More evil is done than can be healed by punishment: men seem engaged in a vast race of wickedness. Every day there is greater eagerness to sin, less modesty. Throwing aside all reverence for what is better and more just, lust rushes whithersoever it thinks fit, and crimes are no longer committed by stealth, they take place before our eyes, and wickedness has become so general and gained such a footing in everyone's breast that innocence is no longer rare, but no longer exists. Do men break the law singly, or a few at a time? Nay, they rise in all quarters at once, as though obeying some universal signal, to wipe out the boundaries of right and wrong.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: A wise man would never stop being angry once he started, because every place is packed with vice and crime. More evil happens than punishment can ever fix. People seem to be racing each other to see who can be most wicked. Each day brings more eagerness to sin and less shame. Throwing aside all respect for what is good and just, lust rushes wherever it wants to go. Crimes are no longer done in secret — they happen right in front of us. Wickedness has become so common and taken such deep root in everyone's hearts that innocence isn't just rare anymore. It no longer exists. Do people break the law one at a time, or just a few together? No, they rise up everywhere at once, as if responding to some universal signal, to erase the line between right and wrong.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: "Host is not safe from guest, Father-in-law from son; but seldom love Exists 'twixt brothers; wives long to destroy Their husbands, husbands long to slay their wives, Stepmothers deadly aconite prepare And child-heirs wonder when their sires will die." And how small a part of men's crimes are these! The poet[5] has not described one people divided into two hostile camps, parents and children enrolled on opposite sides, Rome set on fire by the hand of a Roman, troops of fierce horsemen scouring the country to track out the hiding-places of the proscribed, wells defiled with poison, plagues created by human hands, trenches dug by children round their beleaguered parents, crowded prisons, conflagrations that consume whole cities, gloomy tyrannies, secret plots to establish despotisms and ruin peoples, and men glorying in those deeds which, as long as it was possible to repress them, were counted as crimes—I mean rape, debauchery, and lust . . . . . Add to these, public acts of national bad faith, broken treaties, everything that cannot defend itself carried off as plunder by the stronger, knaveries, thefts, frauds, and disownings of debt such as three of our present law-courts would not suffice to deal with. If you want the wise man to be as angry as the atrocity of men's crimes requires, he must not merely be angry, but must go mad with rage.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "No guest is safe from his host. No father-in-law is safe from his son-in-law. Brothers rarely love each other. Wives want to destroy their husbands. Husbands want to kill their wives. Stepmothers prepare deadly poison. Children wonder when their fathers will finally die." But these crimes are nothing! The poet hasn't described a whole nation split into two enemy camps. He hasn't described parents and children fighting on opposite sides. He hasn't described Rome set on fire by Romans themselves. He hasn't described cavalry troops hunting down the condemned. He hasn't described wells poisoned, plagues created by human hands, children digging trenches around their own besieged parents. He hasn't described packed prisons, cities burned to the ground, dark tyrannies, secret plots to overthrow governments and destroy peoples. He hasn't described men celebrating acts that used to be called crimes — rape, corruption, and lust. Add to this list: nations breaking their word, broken treaties, the strong stealing everything the weak cannot defend, cheating, theft, fraud, and debt dodging so widespread that three courts couldn't handle it all. If you want the wise man to get as angry as human crimes deserve, he wouldn't just be angry. He'd go completely insane with rage.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: You will rather think that we should not be angry with people's faults; for what shall we say of one who is angry with those who stumble in the dark, or with deaf people who cannot hear his orders, or with children, because they forget their duty and interest themselves in the games and silly jokes of their companions? What shall we say if you choose to be angry with weaklings for being sick, for growing old, or becoming fatigued? Among the other misfortunes of humanity is this, that men's intellects are confused, and they not only cannot help going wrong, but love to go wrong. To avoid being angry with individuals, you must pardon the whole mass, you must grant forgiveness to the entire human race. If you are angry with young and old men because they do wrong, you will be angry with infants also, for they soon will do wrong.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: You should think we shouldn't get angry at people's flaws. What would you say about someone who gets mad at people stumbling in the dark? Or at deaf people who can't hear orders? Or at children who forget their duties and get caught up in games and silly jokes with friends? What if you choose to get angry at sick people for being sick, at old people for aging, or at tired people for being tired? Among all the bad things about humanity is this: our minds are confused. We not only can't help making mistakes — we actually love making mistakes. To avoid getting angry at individuals, you have to forgive everyone. You have to grant forgiveness to the entire human race. If you get angry at young and old people for doing wrong, you'll have to be angry at babies too. After all, they'll do wrong soon enough.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Does any one become angry with children, who are too young to comprehend distinctions? Yet, to be a human being is a greater and a better excuse than to be a child. Thus are we born, as creatures liable to as many disorders of the mind as of the body; not dull and slow-witted, but making a bad use of our keenness of wit, and leading one another into vice by our example. He who follows others who have started before him on the wrong road is surely excusable for having wandered on[6] the highway. A general's severity may be shown in the case of individual deserters; but where a whole army deserts, it must needs be pardoned. What is it that puts a stop to the wise man's anger? It is the number of sinners. He perceives how unjust and how dangerous it is to be angry with vices which all men share.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Do you get angry with children who are too young to understand right from wrong? Of course not. But being human is an even better excuse than being a child. We're all born with minds that can go wrong just like our bodies can get sick. We're not stupid or slow — we're actually too clever for our own good. We use our intelligence badly and lead each other astray by our example. If someone follows others who started down the wrong path first, you can hardly blame them for getting lost. A general might punish one deserter harshly, but if the whole army deserts, he has to forgive them all. What stops a wise person from getting angry? The sheer number of people doing wrong. He sees how unfair and dangerous it is to rage against faults that we all share.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Heraclitcus, whenever he came out of doors and beheld around him such a number of men who were living wretchedly, nay, rather perishing wretchedly, used to weep: he pitied all those who met him joyous and happy. He was of a gentle but too weak disposition; and he himself was one of those for whom he ought to have wept. Democritus, on the other hand, is said never to have appeared in public without laughing; so little did men's serious occupations appear serious to him. What room is there for anger? Everything ought either to move us to tears or to laughter. The wise man will not be angry with sinners. Why not? Because he knows that no one is born wise, but becomes so: he knows that very few wise men are produced in any age, because he thoroughly understands the circumstances of human life. Now, no sane man is angry with nature: for what should we say if a man chose to be surprised that fruit did not hang on the thickets of a forest, or to wonder at bushes and thorns not being covered with some useful berry?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Heraclitus used to cry whenever he went outside and saw so many people living miserable lives — or really, dying miserable deaths. He felt sorry for everyone he met who seemed happy and cheerful. He had a gentle heart, but it was too tender for his own good. In fact, he was one of the people he should have been crying for. Democritus was the opposite. He supposedly never appeared in public without laughing. Human affairs struck him as so ridiculous that he couldn't take any of them seriously. So where does that leave room for anger? Everything should either make us laugh or make us cry. A wise person won't get angry at people who do wrong. Why not? Because he knows that nobody is born wise — we have to become wise. He knows that very few people in any generation actually become wise. He understands what human life is really like. No reasonable person gets angry at nature. What would you say about someone who was shocked that fruit trees don't grow wild in the forest? Or someone amazed that thornbushes don't produce useful berries?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: No one is angry when nature excuses a defect. The wise man, therefore, being tranquil, and dealing candidly with mistakes, not an enemy to but an improver of sinners, will go abroad every day in the following frame of mind:—"Many men will meet me who are drunkards, lustful, ungrateful, greedy, and excited by the frenzy of ambition." He will view all these as benignly as a physician does his patients. When a man's ship leaks freely through its opened seams, does he become angry with the sailors or the ship itself? No; instead of that, he tries to remedy it: he shuts out some water, bales out some other, closes all the holes that he can see, and by ceaseless labour counteracts those which are out of sight and which let water into the hold; nor does he relax his efforts because as much water as he pumps out runs in again. We need a long-breathed struggle against permanent and prolific evils; not, indeed, to quell them, but merely to prevent their overpowering us.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: No one gets angry at nature for causing a birth defect. The wise person stays calm and deals honestly with mistakes. He's not an enemy of wrongdoers — he helps them improve. Every day he goes out thinking: "I'll meet many people today who drink too much, who chase sex, who are ungrateful, greedy, and driven mad by ambition." He looks at all of them as kindly as a doctor looks at his patients. When a ship is leaking badly through cracked boards, does the captain get angry at the sailors or the ship? No. Instead, he tries to fix it. He blocks some leaks, bails out water, plugs every hole he can see. He works constantly to fight the hidden leaks that keep flooding the ship. He doesn't give up just because water pours in as fast as he pumps it out. We need a long, steady fight against permanent and endless problems. Not to defeat them completely, but just to keep them from overwhelming us.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: "Anger," says our opponent, "is useful, because it avoids contempt, and because it frightens bad men." Now, in the first place, if anger is strong in proportion to its threats, it is hateful for the same reason that it is terrible: and it is more dangerous to be hated than to be despised. If, again, it is without strength, it is much more exposed to contempt, and cannot avoid ridicule; for what is more flat than anger when it breaks out into meaningless ravings? Moreover, because some things are somewhat terrible, they are not on that account desirable: nor does wisdom wish it to be said of the wise man, as it is of a wild beast, that the fear which he inspires is as a weapon to him. Why, do we not fear fever, gout, consuming ulcers? and is there, for that reason, any good in them? nay; on the other hand, they are all despised and thought to be foul and base, and are for this very reason feared. So, too, anger is in itself hideous and by no means to be feared; yet it is feared by many, just as a hideous mask is feared by children.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "Anger is useful," our opponent says, "because it prevents contempt and frightens bad people." But here's the problem with this argument. First, if anger is powerful because it threatens people, then it's also hateful for the same reason it's scary. And being hated is more dangerous than being looked down on. Second, if anger is weak, it becomes even more contemptible and ridiculous. What's more pathetic than anger that just turns into meaningless ranting? Just because something is frightening doesn't make it good. Wisdom doesn't want people to say about a wise person what they say about a wild animal — that fear is his weapon. We fear fever, gout, and painful sores, but does that make them good? Of course not. We despise these things and think they're disgusting and shameful, which is exactly why we fear them. Anger works the same way. It's ugly and shouldn't be feared, yet many people do fear it — just like children fear a scary mask.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
How can we answer the fact that terror always works back to him who inspired it, and that no one is feared who is himself at peace? At this point it is well that you should remember that verse of Laberius, which, when pronounced in the theatre during the height of the civil war, caught the fancy of the whole people as though it expressed the national feeling:—

"He must fear many, whom so many fear."

Thus has nature ordained, that whatever becomes great by causing fear to others is not free from fear itself. How disturbed lions are at the faintest noises! How excited those fiercest of beasts become at strange shadows, voices, or smells! Whatever is a terror to others, fears for itself. There can be no reason, therefore, for any wise man to wish to be feared, and no one need think that anger is anything great because it strikes terror, since even the most despicable things are feared, as, for example, noxious vermin whose bite is venomous: and since a string set with feathers stops the largest herds of wild beasts and guides them into traps, it is no wonder that from its effect it should be named a "Scarer."[7] Foolish creatures are frightened by foolish things: the movement of chariots and the sight of their wheels turning round drives lions back into their cage: elephants are frightened at the cries of pigs: and so also we fear anger just as children fear the dark, or wild beasts fear red feathers: it has in itself nothing solid or valiant, but it affects feeble minds.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: How can we explain this fact: terror always comes back to haunt whoever creates it. No one who lives in peace is truly feared. Here you should remember that line from Laberius. When it was spoken in the theater during the civil war, the whole audience loved it because it captured how everyone felt: "He must fear many, whom so many fear." This is how nature works. Whatever grows powerful by making others afraid cannot escape fear itself. See how lions jump at the smallest sounds! How the fiercest animals get spooked by unfamiliar shadows, voices, or smells! Whatever terrorizes others lives in terror too. So no wise person should want to be feared. And don't think anger is something great just because it scares people. Even the most worthless things can be frightening — like poisonous bugs whose bite can kill you. A string decorated with feathers can stop entire herds of wild animals and guide them into traps. That's why they call it a "Scarer." Stupid creatures get scared by stupid things. The sound of chariots and sight of spinning wheels drives lions back into their cages. Elephants run from squealing pigs. We fear anger the same way children fear the dark or wild beasts fear red feathers. Anger has nothing solid or brave about it. It only works on weak minds.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: "Wickedness," says our adversary, "must be removed from the system of nature, if you wish to remove anger: neither of which things can be done." In the first place, it is possible for a man not to be cold, although according to the system of nature it may be winter-time, nor yet to suffer from heat, although it be summer according to the almanac. He may be protected against the inclement time of the year by dwelling in a favoured spot, or he may have so trained his body to endurance that it feels neither heat nor cold. Next, reverse this saying:—You must remove anger from your mind before you can take virtue into the same, because vices and virtues cannot combine, and none can at the same time be both an angry man and a good man, any more than he can be both sick and well.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "Evil must be removed from the natural order," says our opponent, "if you want to remove anger. And neither of these things can be done." First, a person can avoid being cold even when it's winter by nature's calendar. They can avoid being hot even when it's summer by the almanac. They might live in a sheltered place, or they might have trained their body to handle extremes so well that they don't feel heat or cold. Now flip this argument around: You must remove anger from your mind before you can let virtue in. Vices and virtues cannot mix. No one can be both angry and good at the same time, any more than someone can be both sick and healthy.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: "It is not possible," says he, "to remove anger altogether from the mind, nor does human nature admit of it." Yet there is nothing so hard and difficult that the mind of man cannot overcome it, and with which unremitting study will not render him familiar, nor are there any passions so fierce and independent that they cannot be tamed by discipline. The mind can carry out whatever orders it gives itself: some have succeeded in never smiling: some have forbidden themselves wine, sexual intercourse, or even drink of all kinds. Some, who are satisfied with short hours of rest, have learned to watch for long periods without weariness. Men have learned to run upon the thinnest ropes even when slanting, to carry huge burdens, scarcely within the compass of human strength, or to dive to enormous depths and suffer themselves to remain under the sea without any chance of drawing breath.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "You can't completely remove anger from the mind," some people say. "Human nature won't allow it." But there's nothing so hard that the human mind can't overcome it. With constant practice, we can master anything. No passion is so wild that discipline can't tame it. The mind can do whatever it commands itself to do. Some people have succeeded in never smiling. Others have given up wine, sex, or even all drinks. Some people who need little sleep have learned to stay awake for long periods without getting tired. People have learned to run on thin ropes, even when they're slanted. They carry huge weights that seem beyond human strength. They dive to incredible depths and hold their breath underwater for impossibly long times.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: There are a thousand other instances in which application has conquered all obstacles, and proved that nothing which the mind has set itself to endure is difficult. The men whom I have just mentioned gain either no reward or one that is unworthy of their unwearied application; for what great thing does a man gain by applying his intellect to walking upon a tight rope? or to placing great burdens upon his shoulders? or to keeping sleep from his eyes? or to reaching the bottom of the sea? and yet their patient labour brings all these things to pass for a trifling reward. Shall not we then call in the aid of patience, we whom such a prize awaits, the unbroken calm of a happy life? How great a blessing is it to escape from anger, that chief of all evils, and therewith from frenzy, ferocity, cruelty, and madness, its attendants?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: There are countless other examples where practice has overcome every obstacle. They prove that nothing is too hard if your mind is set on enduring it. The men I just mentioned get either no reward or one that hardly matches their endless effort. What great thing does someone gain by learning to walk on a tightrope? Or by carrying heavy weights on their shoulders? Or by staying awake for days? Or by diving to the bottom of the sea? Yet their patient work makes all these things possible — for almost nothing in return. So shouldn't we use that same patience when such a prize awaits us: the unbroken calm of a happy life? What a blessing it would be to escape from anger, the worst of all evils, and along with it from frenzy, cruelty, and madness — all its companions.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
There is no reason why we should seek to defend such a passion
as this or excuse its excesses by declaring it to be either useful
or unavoidable. What vice, indeed, is without its defenders? yet
this is no reason why you should declare anger to be ineradicable.
The evils from which we suffer are curable, and since we were born
with a natural bias towards good, nature herself will help us if
we try to amend our lives. Nor is the path to virtue steep and
rough, as some think it to be: it may be reached on level ground.
This is no untrue tale which I come to tell you: the road to happiness
is easy; do you only enter upon it with good luck and the good help
of the gods themselves. It is much harder to do what you are doing.
What is more restful than a mind at peace, and what more toilsome
than anger? What is more at leisure than clemency, what fuller of
business than cruelty? Modesty keeps holiday while vice is overwhelmed
with work. In fine, the culture of any of the virtues is easy, while
vices require a great expense. Anger ought to be removed from our
minds: even those who say that it ought to be kept low admit this
to some extent: let it be got rid of altogether; there is nothing
to be gained by it. Without it we can more easily and more justly
put an end to crime, punish bad men, and amend their lives.
The wise man will do his duty in all things without the help of any
evil passion, and will use no auxiliaries which require watching
narrowly lest they get beyond his control.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: There's no point in defending anger or making excuses for it. Don't tell me it's useful or unavoidable. Every vice has its defenders — that doesn't make anger something we can't overcome. The problems we face can be fixed. We were born with a natural pull toward good, and nature will help us if we actually try to improve. The path to virtue isn't steep and rough like some people think. You can reach it on level ground. I'm telling you the truth here: the road to happiness is easy. You just need to start walking it with some luck and divine help. What you're doing now is much harder work. What's more peaceful than a calm mind? What's more exhausting than anger? What's more relaxed than mercy? What's busier than cruelty? Good behavior takes a holiday while vice works overtime. Bottom line: any virtue is easy to develop, but vices cost you dearly. We need to remove anger from our minds completely. Even people who say we should just keep it under control are admitting this partly. Get rid of it entirely — there's nothing good it does for you. Without anger, we can stop crime more easily and fairly. We can punish bad people and help them change. A wise person will do what's right without any evil passion helping him. He won't use tools that need constant watching to keep them from spinning out of control.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Anger, then, must never become a habit with us, but we may
sometimes affect to be angry when we wish to rouse up the dull minds
of those whom we address, just as we rouse up horses who are slow
at starting with goads and firebrands. We must sometimes apply fear
to persons upon whom reason makes no impression: yet to be angry
is of no more use than to grieve or to be afraid. “What? do not
circumstances arise which provoke us to anger?” Yes: but at those
times above all others we ought to choke down our wrath. Nor is it
difficult to conquer our spirit, seeing that athletes, who devote
their whole attention to the basest parts of themselves, nevertheless
are able to endure blows and pain, in order to exhaust the strength
of the striker, and do not strike when anger bids them, but when
opportunity invites them. It is said that Pyrrhus, the most celebrated
trainer for gymnastic contests, used habitually to impress upon his
pupils not to lose their tempers: for anger spoils their science,
and thinks only how it can hurt: so that often reason counsels
patience while anger counsels revenge, and we, who might have
survived our first misfortunes, are exposed to worse ones. Some
have been driven into exile by their impatience of a single
contemptuous word, have been plunged into the deepest miseries
because they would not endure the most trifling wrong in silence,
and have brought upon themselves the yoke of slavery because they
were too proud to give up the least part of their entire liberty.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Anger should never become a habit. But sometimes we can pretend to be angry when we need to wake up people who aren't paying attention — like using spurs and torches to get lazy horses moving. Sometimes we need to use fear on people who won't listen to reason. But actually being angry is as useless as grieving or being afraid. "But don't some situations naturally make us angry?" Yes — and those are exactly the times we most need to control our rage. It's not that hard to master our emotions. Athletes focus on the crudest parts of training, yet they can take punches and pain to wear down their opponent. They don't strike when anger tells them to, but when the right moment comes. Pyrrhus, the most famous athletic trainer, always told his students not to lose their tempers. Anger ruins technique and only thinks about causing harm. Reason often tells us to wait, while anger demands revenge. People who might have survived their first troubles get hit with worse ones. Some have been exiled because they couldn't stand a single insult. Others have fallen into deep misery because they wouldn't quietly endure the smallest slight. They've brought slavery upon themselves because they were too proud to give up even a tiny bit of their freedom.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“That you may be sure,” says our opponent, “that anger has in
it something noble, pray look at the free nations, such as the
Germans and Scythians, who are especially prone to anger.” The
reason of this is that stout and daring intellects are liable
to anger before they are tamed by discipline; for some passions
engraft themselves upon the better class of dispositions only, just
as good land, even when waste, grows strong brushwood, and the trees
are tall which stand upon a fertile soil. In like manner, dispositions
which are naturally bold produce irritability, and, being hot and
fiery, have no mean or trivial qualities, but their energy is
misdirected, as happens with all those who without training come
to the front by their natural advantages alone, whose minds, unless
they be brought under control, degenerate from a courageous temper
into habits of rashness and reckless daring. “What? are not milder
spirits linked with gentler vices, such as tenderness of heart,
love, and bashfulness?” Yes, and therefore I can often point out
to you a good disposition by its own faults: yet their being the
proofs of a superior nature does not prevent their being vices.
Moreover, all those nations which are free because they are wild,
like lions or wolves, cannot command any more than they can obey:
for the strength of their intellect is not civilized, but fierce
and unmanageable: now, no one is able to rule unless he is also
able to be ruled. Consequently, the empire of the world has almost
always remained in the hands of those nations who enjoy a milder
climate. Those who dwell near the frozen north have uncivilized
tempers—

“Just on the model of their native skies,”

as the poet has it.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "To prove that anger has something noble about it," our opponent says, "just look at free nations like the Germans and Scythians. They're especially quick to anger." But here's why that happens: bold and daring minds are prone to anger before they learn discipline. Some emotions only take root in better types of people — just like good land, even when it's wild, grows strong weeds and tall trees in rich soil. In the same way, naturally bold personalities create irritability. Being hot and fiery, they have nothing weak or petty about them. But their energy goes in the wrong direction. This happens to everyone who rises by natural talent alone without training. Unless these minds are controlled, they fall from courage into reckless, dangerous habits. "But aren't gentler spirits connected to gentler vices, like being too soft-hearted, too loving, or too shy?" Yes — and that's why I can often spot a good nature by its very flaws. But just because these flaws prove someone has a superior nature doesn't mean they're not still vices. Besides, all those nations that are free because they're wild — like lions or wolves — can't command any more than they can obey. Their mental strength isn't civilized but fierce and uncontrollable. And no one can rule unless they can also be ruled. So the world's great empires have almost always stayed in the hands of nations with milder climates. Those who live near the frozen north have uncivilized tempers — "just like their native skies," as the poet says.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Those animals, urges our opponent, are held to be the most
generous who have large capacity for anger. He is mistaken when he
holds up creatures who act from impulse instead of reason as patterns
for men to follow, because in man reason takes the place of impulse.
Yet even with animals, all do not alike profit by the same thing.
Anger is of use to lions, timidity to stags, boldness to hawks,
flight to doves. What if I declare that it is not even true that
the best animals are the most prone to anger? I may suppose that
wild beasts, who gain their food by rapine, are better the angrier
they are; but I should praise oxen and horses who obey the rein for
their patience. What reason, however, have you for referring mankind
to such wretched models, when you have the universe and God, whom
he alone of animals imitates because he alone comprehends Him? “The
most irritable men,” says he, “are thought to be the most straightforward
of all.” Yes, because they are compared with swindlers and sharpers,
and appear to be simple because they are outspoken. I should not
call such men simple, but heedless. We give this title of “simple”
to all fools, gluttons, spendthrifts, and men whose vices lie on
the surface.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: My opponent argues that the most noble animals are those with great capacity for anger. He's wrong to hold up creatures who act on impulse rather than reason as examples for humans to follow. In humans, reason replaces impulse. Even with animals, not all benefit from the same traits. Anger helps lions, timidity helps deer, boldness helps hawks, and flight helps doves. But I'll go further — it's not even true that the best animals are the angriest. Wild beasts that hunt for food might be better when they're angry, but I'd praise patient oxen and horses who obey the reins. Why would you point humans toward such poor examples when you have the universe and God as models? Humans alone can imitate God because we alone understand Him. "The most hot-tempered people," my opponent says, "are thought to be the most honest." Sure — compared to cheats and con artists, they seem simple because they speak their minds. I wouldn't call such people simple, just careless. We use the word "simple" for all kinds of fools — gluttons, spendthrifts, and people whose vices are obvious.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“An orator,” says our opponent, “sometimes speaks better,
when he is angry.” Not so, but when he pretends to be angry: for
so also actors bring down the house by their playing, not when they
are really angry, but when they act the angry man well: and in like
manner, in addressing a jury or a popular assembly, or in any other
position in which the minds of others have to be influenced at our
pleasure, we must ourselves pretend to feel anger, fear, or pity
before we can make others feel them, and often the pretence of
passion will do what the passion itself could not have done. “The
mind which does not feel anger,” says he, “is feeble.” True, if it
has nothing stronger than anger to support it. A man ought to be
neither robber nor victim, neither tender-hearted nor cruel. The
former belongs to an over-weak mind, the latter to an over-hard
one. Let the wise man be moderate, and when things have to be done
somewhat briskly, let him call force, not anger, to his aid.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "An orator speaks better when he's angry," our opponent says. Not true. He speaks better when he pretends to be angry. Actors bring down the house with their performances — not when they're actually angry, but when they act anger well. It's the same when addressing a jury or crowd. When you need to influence people, you must pretend to feel anger, fear, or pity before you can make others feel them. Often the pretense of passion works better than real passion ever could. "A mind that doesn't feel anger is weak," he says. True — if it has nothing stronger than anger to rely on. A person should be neither robber nor victim, neither soft-hearted nor cruel. The first comes from a too-weak mind, the second from a too-hard one. Let the wise person be moderate. When action is needed, let him use force — not anger.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Now that we have discussed the questions propounded concerning
anger, let us pass on to the consideration of its remedies.
These, I imagine, are two-fold: the one class preventing our becoming
angry, the other preventing our doing wrong when we are angry. As
