with the body we adopt a certain regimen to keep ourselves in health,
and use different rules to bring back health when lost, so likewise
we must repel anger in one fashion and quench it in another. That
we may avoid it, certain general rules of conduct which apply to
all men’s lives must be impressed upon us. We may divide these into
such as are of use during the education of the young and in after-life.

Education ought to be carried on with the greatest and most salutary
assiduity: for it is easy to mould minds while they are still tender,
but it is difficult to uproot vices which have grown up with
ourselves.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
Now that we've talked about the nature of anger, let's move on to its remedies. I think there are two kinds: one to prevent us from getting angry in the first place, and another to prevent us from doing harm once we're already angry. Just like we follow one set of health rules to stay well and different rules to recover when we're sick, we need different approaches to ward off anger and to calm it down. To avoid anger altogether, we need certain general principles that apply to everyone's life. We can divide these into lessons for educating the young and guidelines for adult life.

Education should be handled with the greatest care and persistence. It's easy to shape minds while they're still soft, but it's hard to tear out bad habits that have grown up with us.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: A hot mind is naturally the most prone to anger: for as there are four elements,[8] consisting of fire, air, earth, and water, so there are powers corresponding and equivalent to each of these, namely, hot, cold, dry, and moist. Now the mixture of the elements is the cause of the diversities of lands and of animals, of bodies and of character, and our dispositions incline to one or the other of these according as the strength of each element prevails in us. Hence it is that we call some regions wet or dry, warm or cold. The same distinctions apply likewise to animals and mankind; it makes a great difference how much moisture or heat a man contains; his character will partake of whichever element has the largest share in him.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: A hot temperament is naturally most prone to anger. Just as there are four elements — fire, air, earth, and water — there are four corresponding qualities: hot, cold, dry, and moist. The way these elements mix determines the differences between lands, animals, bodies, and personalities. Our dispositions lean toward whichever element is strongest in us. This is why we call some regions wet or dry, warm or cold. The same applies to animals and people. It makes a huge difference how much moisture or heat a person contains. Their character will reflect whichever element dominates them.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: A warm temper of mind will make men prone to anger; for fire is full of movement and vigour; a mixture of coldness makes men cowards, for cold is sluggish and contracted. Because of this, some of our Stoics think that anger is excited in our breasts by the boiling of the blood round the heart: indeed, that place is assigned to anger for no other reason than because the breast is the warmest part of the whole body. Those who have more moisture in them become angry by slow degrees, because they have no heat ready at hand, but it has to be obtained by movement; wherefore the anger of women and children is sharp rather than strong, and arises on lighter provocation. At dry times of life anger is violent and powerful, yet without increase, and adding little to itself, because as heat dies away cold takes its place. Old men are testy and full of complaints, as also are sick people and convalescents, and all whose store of heat has been consumed by weariness or loss of blood. Those who are wasted by thirst or hunger are in the same condition, as also are those whose frame is naturally bloodless and faints from want of generous diet. Wine kindles anger, because it increases heat; according to each man's disposition, some fly into a passion when they are heavily drunk, some when they are slightly drunk: nor is there any other reason than this why yellow-haired, ruddy-complexioned people should be excessively passionate, seeing that they are naturally of the colour which others put on during anger; for their blood is hot and easily set in motion.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
People with hot temperaments get angry easily. Fire is full of movement and energy. Cold makes people cowardly, because cold is slow and stiff. Some of our Stoic philosophers think anger happens when blood boils around the heart. They say this is why we feel anger in our chest — because the chest is the warmest part of the body.

People with more moisture in them get angry slowly. They don't have heat ready to go, so they need movement to build it up. That's why women and children have sharp anger rather than strong anger. It flares up over small things.

In the dry times of life, anger is violent and powerful. But it doesn't grow much, because as heat fades, cold takes over. Old people are cranky and complain a lot. So do sick people and those recovering from illness. Anyone whose heat has been drained by exhaustion or blood loss acts this way.

People wasted by thirst or hunger are the same. So are those who are naturally pale and weak from poor diet. Wine sparks anger because it increases heat. Depending on the person, some explode when very drunk, others when just slightly drunk. This is also why blonde, red-faced people are so passionate. They naturally have the color that others turn when angry. Their blood is hot and easily stirred up.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
But just as nature makes some men prone to anger, so there are
many other causes which have the same power as nature. Some are
brought into this condition by disease or bodily injury, others by
hard work, long watching, nights of anxiety, ardent longings, and
love: and everything else which is hurtful to the body or the spirit
inclines the distempered mind to find fault. All these, however,
are but the beginning and causes of anger. Habit of mind has very
great power, and, if it be harsh, increases the disorder. As
for nature, it is difficult to alter it, nor may we change the
mixture of the elements which was formed once for all at our birth:
yet knowledge will be so far of service, that we should keep wine
out of the reach of hot-tempered men, which Plato thinks ought also
to be forbidden to boys, so that fire be not made fiercer.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Just as nature makes some people naturally angry, many other things can do the same damage. Some people become angry from illness or injury. Others from overwork, sleepless nights, worry, passionate desires, and love. Anything that hurts the body or mind makes a troubled person more likely to complain. But these are just the triggers and causes of anger. Your mental habits have enormous power. If your habits are harsh, they make the problem worse. As for your nature — that's hard to change. We can't alter the mix of elements we were born with. But knowledge helps this much: we should keep wine away from hot-tempered people. Plato thought boys shouldn't drink either, so we don't add fire to fire.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Neither
should such men be over-fed: for if so, their bodies will swell,
and their minds will swell with them. Such men ought to take exercise,
stopping short, however, of fatigue, in order that their natural
heat may be abated, but not exhausted, and their excess of fiery
spirit may be worked off. Games also will be useful: for moderate
pleasure relieves the mind and brings it to a proper balance. With
those temperaments which incline to moisture, or dryness and
stiffness, there is no danger of anger, but there is fear of greater
vices, such as cowardice, moroseness, despair, and suspiciousness:
such dispositions therefore ought to be softened, comforted, and
restored to cheerfulness: and since we must make use of different
remedies for anger and for sullenness, and these two vices require
not only unlike, but absolutely opposite modes of treatment, let
us always attack that one of them which is gaining the mastery.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Don't overfeed these men either. If you do, their bodies will get bigger, and their minds will get bigger with them. Such men should exercise, but not to the point of exhaustion. This will cool down their natural heat without draining it completely. It will also work off their excess fiery energy. Games will help too. Moderate pleasure calms the mind and brings it into balance. People with temperaments that lean toward moisture, dryness, or stiffness don't risk anger. But they do risk worse vices — cowardice, gloominess, despair, and suspicion. These types need to be softened, comforted, and cheered up. We need different remedies for anger versus sullenness. These two vices need not just different treatments, but completely opposite ones. So let's always attack whichever vice is winning.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: It is, I assure you, of the greatest service to boys that they should be soundly brought up, yet to regulate their education is difficult, because it is our duty to be careful neither to cherish a habit of anger in them, nor to blunt the edge of their spirit. This needs careful watching, for both qualities, both those which are to be encouraged, and those which are to be checked, are fed by the same things; and even a careful watcher may be deceived by their likeness. A boy's spirit is increased by freedom and depressed by slavery: it rises when praised, and is led to conceive great expectations of itself: yet this same treatment produces arrogance and quickness of temper: we must therefore guide him between these two extremes, using the curb at one time and the spur at another.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: I promise you, it's incredibly important that boys get a solid upbringing. But managing their education is tricky. We need to be careful not to encourage anger in them, while also not crushing their spirit. This requires constant attention. The qualities we want to build up and the ones we want to control are often fed by the same things. Even when you're watching closely, you can be fooled by how similar they look. A boy's spirit grows when he has freedom and shrinks when he's treated like a slave. He rises when praised and starts to expect great things from himself. But this same treatment can also create arrogance and a quick temper. So we have to guide him between these two extremes — sometimes holding him back, sometimes pushing him forward.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: He must undergo no servile or degrading treatment; he never must beg abjectly for anything, nor must he gain anything by begging; let him rather receive it for his own sake, for his past good behaviour, or for his promises of future good conduct. In contests with his comrades we ought not to allow him to become sulky or fly into a passion: let us see that he be on friendly terms with those whom he contends with, so that in the struggle itself he may learn to wish not to hurt his antagonist but to conquer him: whenever he has gained the day or done something praiseworthy, we should allow him to enjoy his victory, but not to rush into transports of delight: for joy leads to exultation, and exultation leads to swaggering and excessive self-esteem, We ought to allow him some relaxation, yet not yield him up to laziness and sloth, and we ought to keep him far beyond the reach of luxury, for nothing makes children more prone to anger than a soft and fond bringing-up, so that the more only children are indulged, and the more liberty is given to orphans, the more they are corrupted.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: He should never have to put up with harsh or humiliating treatment. He should never have to beg pathetically for anything, and he shouldn't get things by begging. Instead, let him earn things because of who he is, his past good behavior, or his promises to do better in the future. When he competes with other children, don't let him sulk or lose his temper. Make sure he stays on good terms with his competitors. That way, during the contest itself, he learns to want victory — not to hurt his opponent. When he wins or does something worth praising, let him enjoy his success. But don't let him get carried away with excitement. Joy leads to showing off, and showing off leads to arrogance and thinking too highly of yourself. Give him some downtime, but don't let him become lazy and idle. Keep him far away from luxury. Nothing makes children more likely to get angry than soft, spoiled upbringing. The more you pamper an only child, and the more freedom you give orphans, the more you ruin them.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: He to whom nothing is ever denied, will not be able to endure a rebuff, whose anxious mother always wipes away his tears, whose _paedagogus_[9] is made to pay for his shortcomings. Do you not observe how a man's anger becomes more violent as he rises in station? This shows itself especially in those that are rich and noble, or in great place, when the favouring gale has roused all the most empty and trivial passions of their minds. Prosperity fosters anger, when a man's proud ears are surrounded by a mob of flatterers, saying, "That man answer you! you do not act according to your dignity, you lower yourself." And so forth, with all the language which can hardly be resisted even by healthy and originally well-principled minds. Flattery, then, must be kept well out of the way of children. Let a child hear the truth, and sometimes fear it: let him always reverence it. Let him rise in the presence of his elders.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: A child who is never told "no" won't be able to handle rejection when he grows up. His worried mother always dries his tears. His tutor gets punished for the child's mistakes. Haven't you noticed how people get angrier as they gain more power? This is especially true for the rich, the well-born, and those in high positions. When success fills their sails, it stirs up all the most shallow and petty emotions in their minds. Success feeds anger. A person's proud ears get surrounded by crowds of flatterers who say things like: "How dare he talk to you that way! You're not acting with proper dignity! You're lowering yourself!" And so on, with all the words that even healthy, well-principled minds can barely resist. So keep flattery far away from children. Let a child hear the truth, and sometimes be afraid of it. Let him always respect it. Let him stand up when his elders enter the room.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Let him obtain nothing by flying into a passion: let him be given when he is quiet what was refused him when he cried for it: let him behold, but not make use of his father's wealth: let him be reproved for what he does wrong. It will be advantageous to furnish boys with even-tempered teachers and _paedagogi_: what is soft and unformed clings to what is near, and takes its shape: the habits of young men reproduce those of their nurses and _paedagogi_. Once, a boy who was brought up in Plato's house went home to his parents, and, on seeing his father shouting with passion, said, "I never saw any one at Plato's house act like that." I doubt not that he learned to imitate his father sooner than he learned to imitate Plato. Above all, let his food be scanty, his dress not costly, and of the same fashion as that of his comrades: if you begin by putting him on a level with many others, he will not be angry when some one is compared with him.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Don't give him what he wants when he throws a tantrum. Give it to him when he's calm and asks nicely. Let him see his father's wealth but not use it freely. Correct him when he does wrong. It helps to give boys teachers and tutors who stay calm and even-tempered. Children are like soft clay — they stick to whatever is nearby and take that shape. Young people copy the habits of their nurses and tutors. Once, a boy raised in Plato's house went home to his parents. When he saw his father shouting angrily, he said, "I never saw anyone at Plato's house act like that." I'm sure he learned to copy his father faster than he learned to copy Plato. Most importantly, keep his food simple, his clothes inexpensive, and the same style as his friends wear. If you start by putting him on equal footing with others, he won't get angry when someone compares him to them.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
These precepts, however, apply to our children: in ourselves
the accident of birth and our education no longer admits of either
mistakes or advice; we must deal with what follows. Now we ought
to fight against the first causes of evil: the cause of anger is
the belief that we are injured; this belief, therefore, should not
be lightly entertained. We ought not to fly into a rage even when
the injury appears to be open and distinct: for some false things
bear the semblance of truth. We should always allow some time to
elapse, for time discloses the truth. Let not our ears be easily
lent to calumnious talk: let us know and be on our guard against
this fault of human nature, that we are willing to believe what we
are unwilling to listen to, and that we become angry before we have
formed our opinion. What shall I say? we are influenced not
merely by calumnies but by suspicions, and at the very look and
smile of others we may fly into a rage with innocent persons because
we put the worst construction upon it. We ought, therefore, to plead
the cause of the absent against ourselves, and to keep our anger
in abeyance: for a punishment which has been postponed may yet be
inflicted, but when once inflicted cannot be recalled.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: This advice works for our children. But for us adults, our upbringing and education are already done. We can't change our mistakes or take advice the same way. We have to work with what we've got now. We need to fight the root causes of anger. Anger starts when we believe someone has hurt us. So we shouldn't jump to that conclusion too quickly. We shouldn't get furious even when the injury seems obvious and clear. Some lies look like truth. We should always wait a bit. Time reveals what really happened. Don't listen too easily to gossip and accusations. We need to know this flaw in human nature: we want to believe things we don't want to hear. We get angry before we even know what we think. What can I say? We're swayed not just by slander but by suspicions. We might rage at innocent people just because of how they looked at us or smiled. We put the worst spin on everything. So we should defend the person who isn't here to defend themselves. Keep our anger on hold. You can always punish someone later, but once you've done it, you can't take it back.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Every one knows the story of the tyrannicide who, being
caught before he had accomplished his task, and being tortured by
Hippias to make him betray his accomplices, named the friends of
the tyrant who stood around, and every one to whom he knew the
tyrant’s safety was especially dear. As the tyrant ordered each man
to be slain as he was named, at last the man, being asked if any
one else remained, said, “You remain alone, for I have left no one
else alive to whom you are dear.” Anger had made the tyrant lend
his assistance to the tyrant-slayer, and cut down his guards with
his own sword. How far more spirited was Alexander, who after reading
his mother’s letter warning him to beware of poison from his physician
Philip, nevertheless drank undismayed the medicine which Philip
gave him! He felt more confidence in his friend: he deserved that
his friend should be innocent, and deserved that his conduct should
make him innocent. I praise Alexander’s doing this all the more
because he was above all men prone to anger; but the rarer moderation
is among kings, the more it deserves to be praised. The great Gaius
Caesar, who proved such a merciful conqueror in the civil war, did
the same thing; he burned a packet of letters addressed to Gnaeus
Pompeius by persons who had been thought to be either neutrals or
on the other side. Though he was never violent in his anger, yet
he preferred to put it out of his power to be angry: he thought
that the kindest way to pardon each of them was not to know what
his offence had been.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
Everyone knows the story of the would-be assassin who was caught before he could kill the tyrant. Under torture, Hippias tried to make him reveal his partners in the plot. But the assassin was clever. He named the tyrant's own friends — the very people standing around who cared most about keeping the tyrant alive. As the tyrant ordered each friend killed, the assassin was asked if anyone else remained. "Just you," he said. "I've killed everyone else who cared about you." The tyrant's anger had turned him into his own assassin's helper. He had cut down his own guards with his own sword.

How much braver was Alexander! His mother wrote warning him that his doctor Philip might poison him. But when Philip offered him medicine, Alexander drank it without fear. He trusted his friend completely. He deserved to have an innocent friend, and his trust helped make Philip worthy of it. I admire this even more because Alexander was naturally quick to anger. But rare self-control in kings deserves extra praise.

The great Julius Caesar did something similar during the civil war. He burned a whole packet of letters that people had written to Pompey — people who were supposed to be neutral or on Caesar's side. Caesar was rarely violent in his anger, but he chose to make anger impossible. He thought the kindest way to pardon people was simply not to know what they had done wrong.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Readiness to believe what we hear causes very great mischief;
we ought often not even to listen, because in some cases it is
better to be deceived than to suspect deceit. We ought to free our
minds of suspicion and mistrust, those most untrustworthy causes
of anger. “This man’s greeting was far from civil; that one would
not receive my kiss; one cut short a story I had begun to tell;
another did not ask me to dinner; another seemed to view me with
aversion.” Suspicion will never lack grounds: what we want is
straightforwardness, and a kindly interpretation of things. Let us
believe nothing unless it forces itself upon our sight and is
unmistakable, and let us reprove ourselves for being too ready to
believe, as often as our suspicions prove to be groundless: for
this discipline will render us habitually slow to believe what we
hear.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Being too quick to believe what we hear causes huge problems. Often we shouldn't even listen — sometimes it's better to be fooled than to live in constant suspicion. We need to clear our minds of suspicion and mistrust. These are the most unreliable sources of anger. "That person's greeting was cold. This one wouldn't let me kiss them hello. Someone cut me off mid-story. Another person didn't invite me to dinner. That one looked at me with disgust." Suspicion will always find reasons to exist. What we need instead is honesty and a generous way of seeing things. Let's believe nothing unless it's right in front of us and impossible to deny. And whenever our suspicions turn out to be wrong, let's scold ourselves for being too ready to believe them. This practice will make us naturally slow to believe what we hear.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Another consequence of this will be, that we shall not be
exasperated by the slightest and most contemptible trifles. It is
mere madness to be put out of temper because a slave is not quick,
because the water we are going to drink is lukewarm, or because our
couch is disarranged or our table carelessly laid. A man must be
in a miserably bad state of health if he shrinks from a gentle
breath of wind; his eyes must be diseased if they are distressed
by the sight of white clothing; he must be broken down with debauchery
if he feels pain at seeing another man work. It is said that there
was one Mindyrides, a citizen of Sybaris, who one day seeing a man
digging and vigorously brandishing a mattock, complained that the
sight made him weary, and forbade the man to work where he could
see him. The same man complained that he had suffered from the
rose-leaves upon which he lay being folded double.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Another benefit of controlling your anger is that you won't get furious over tiny, worthless things. It's pure madness to lose your temper because a slave is slow, because your drinking water is lukewarm, or because your bed is messy or your table carelessly set. A man must be in terrible health if he flinches at a gentle breeze. His eyes must be diseased if white clothing hurts them. He must be completely worn out by excess if watching another person work causes him pain. They say there was once a man named Mindyrides from Sybaris who saw a worker digging and swinging his pickaxe hard. Mindyrides complained that just watching made him tired, and he told the man to stop working where he could see him. This same man once complained that he couldn't sleep because the rose petals under him had been folded in half.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
When pleasures
have corrupted both the body and the mind, nothing seems endurable,
not indeed because it is hard, but because he who has to bear it
is soft: for why should we be driven to frenzy by any one’s
coughing and sneezing, or by a fly not being driven away with
sufficient care, or by a dog’s hanging about us, or a key dropping
from a careless servant’s hand? Will one whose ears are agonised
by the noise of a bench being dragged along the floor be able to
endure with unruffled mind the rude language of party strife, and
the abuse which speakers in the forum or the senate house heap upon
their opponents? Will he who is angry with his slave for icing his
drink badly, be able to endure hunger, or the thirst of a long march
in summer? Nothing, therefore, nourishes anger more than excessive
and dissatisfied luxury: the mind ought to be hardened by rough
treatment, so as not to feel any blow that is not severe.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: When pleasures corrupt both body and mind, nothing seems bearable — not because it's actually hard, but because the person suffering has gone soft. Why should anyone's coughing or sneezing drive us into a rage? Why get furious when a fly isn't swatted quickly enough, or when a dog follows us around, or when a careless servant drops a key? If someone can't stand the sound of a bench scraping across the floor, how will they handle the rough language of political fights? How will they endure the insults that speakers hurl at each other in courts and government buildings? If you get angry at your slave for not cooling your drink properly, how will you handle real hunger or the thirst of a long summer march? Nothing feeds anger more than too much luxury and never being satisfied. Your mind needs to be toughened by hardship, so that only serious blows can hurt you.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
We are angry, either with those who can, or with those who
cannot do us an injury. To the latter class belong some inanimate
things, such as a book, which we often throw away when it is written
in letters too small for us to read, or tear up when it is full of
mistakes, or clothes which we destroy because we do not like them.
How foolish to be angry with such things as these, which neither
deserve nor feel our anger! “But of course it is their makers who
really affront us.” I answer that, in the first place, we often
become angry before making this distinction clear in our minds, and
secondly, perhaps even the makers might put forward some reasonable
excuses: one of them, it may be, could not make them any better
than he did, and it is not through any disrespect to you that he
was unskilled in his trade: another may have done his work so without
any intention of insulting you: and, finally, what can be more crazy
than to discharge upon things the ill-feeling which one has accumulated
against persons?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: We get angry with people who can hurt us and people who can't hurt us. In the second group are things like books — which we throw away when the letters are too small to read, or tear up when they're full of mistakes. Or clothes that we destroy because we don't like them. How foolish to get angry at things that don't deserve our anger and can't even feel it! "But of course it's really the people who made these things who are insulting us." Here's my answer: First, we often get angry before we even think this through clearly. Second, maybe the makers have good reasons. One person might not have been able to do any better — his lack of skill isn't meant as disrespect to you. Another person might have done sloppy work without any intention of insulting you. And finally, what could be crazier than taking out your anger at people by attacking their products?

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Yet as it is the act of a madman to be angry with
inanimate objects, so also is it to be angry with dumb animals,
which can do us no wrong because they are not able to form a
purpose; and we cannot call anything a wrong unless it be done
intentionally. They are, therefore, able to hurt us, just as a sword
or a stone may do so, but they are not able to do us a wrong. Yet
some men think themselves insulted when the same horses which are
docile with one rider are restive with another, as though it were
through their deliberate choice, and not through habit and cleverness
of handling that some horses are more easily managed by some men
than by others. And as it is foolish to be angry with them, so it
is to be angry with children, and with men who have little more
sense than children: for all these sins, before a just judge,
ignorance would be as effective an excuse as innocence.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: It's crazy to get angry at objects that can't think. It's just as crazy to get angry at animals. They can't do anything wrong because they can't plan to hurt you. Something is only wrong if it's done on purpose. Animals can hurt us, just like a sword or stone can hurt us. But they can't actually wrong us. Some people feel insulted when horses that behave well with one rider act up with another. They think the horse chose to be difficult. But it's really just about habit and how skillfully each person handles the horse. Getting angry at animals is foolish. So is getting angry at children, or at adults who have the sense of children. Before a fair judge, ignorance would excuse all these mistakes just as well as innocence would.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
There are some things which are unable to hurt us, and whose
power is exclusively beneficial and salutary, as, for example, the
immortal gods, who neither wish nor are able to do harm: for their
temperament is naturally gentle and tranquil, and no more likely
to wrong others than to wrong themselves. Foolish people who know
not the truth hold them answerable for storms at sea, excessive
rain, and long winters, whereas all the while these phenomena by
which we suffer or profit take place without any reference whatever
to us: it is not for our sake that the universe causes summer and
winter to succeed one another; these have a law of their own,
according to which their divine functions are performed. We think
too much of ourselves, when we imagine that we are worthy to have
such prodigious revolutions effected for our sake: so, then, none
of these things take place in order to do us an injury, nay, on the
contrary, they all tend to our benefit. I have said that there are
some things which cannot hurt us, and some which would not. To the
latter class belong good men in authority, good parents, teachers,
and judges whose punishments ought to be submitted to by us in the
same spirit in which we undergo the surgeon’s knife, abstinence
from food, and such like things which hurt us for our benefit.
Suppose that we are being punished; let us think not only of what
we suffer, but of what we have done: let us sit in judgement on our
past life. Provided we are willing to tell ourselves the truth, we
shall certainly decide that our crimes deserve a harder measure
than they have received.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Some things simply cannot hurt us. Their power exists only to help and heal us. Take the immortal gods, for example. They neither want to harm us nor can they. Their nature is naturally gentle and peaceful. They are no more likely to wrong others than to wrong themselves. Foolish people who don't understand the truth blame the gods for storms at sea, too much rain, and long winters. But all these things that help us or hurt us happen without any thought of us at all. The universe doesn't create summer and winter for our sake. These seasons follow their own laws. They carry out their divine functions according to their own nature. We think too highly of ourselves when we imagine we're important enough to have such massive forces working just for us. So none of these things happen to hurt us. In fact, they all work toward our benefit. I said there are some things that cannot hurt us, and some that would not want to. Good people in positions of authority belong to this second group. Good parents, teachers, and judges all fall into this category. We should accept their punishments in the same spirit we accept a surgeon's knife, fasting, and other things that hurt us for our own good. Suppose we are being punished. Let's think not only about what we're suffering, but about what we've done. Let's sit in judgment of our past life. If we're willing to tell ourselves the truth, we'll certainly decide that our crimes deserve harsher treatment than we've received.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: If we desire to be impartial judges of all that takes place, we must first convince ourselves of this, that no one of us is faultless: for it is from this that most of our indignation proceeds. "I have not sinned, I have done no wrong." Say, rather, you do not admit that you have done any wrong. We are infuriated at being reproved, either by reprimand or actual chastisement, although we are sinning at that very time, by adding insolence and obstinacy to our wrong-doings. Who is there that can declare himself to have broken no laws? Even if there be such a man, what a stinted innocence it is, merely to be innocent by the letter of the law. How much further do the rules of duty extend than those of the law! how many things which are not to be found in the statute book, are demanded by filial feeling, kindness, generosity, equity, and honour? Yet we are not able to warrant ourselves even to come under that first narrowest definition of innocence: we have done what was wrong, thought what was wrong, wished for what was wrong, and encouraged what was wrong: in some cases we have only remained innocent because we did not succeed.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: If we want to judge situations fairly, we must first accept this truth: none of us is without fault. Most of our anger comes from forgetting this fact. "I haven't sinned. I've done nothing wrong." You should say instead: "I won't admit I've done anything wrong." We get furious when someone corrects us, whether with words or punishment. Yet at that very moment, we're making things worse by being arrogant and stubborn. Who can honestly say they've never broken any laws? And even if someone could claim that, what a narrow kind of innocence that would be — just barely staying legal. The rules of right and wrong go so much further than written laws. Think of all the things not in any law book that duty demands: love for family, kindness, generosity, fairness, honor. Yet we can't even meet that first, most basic definition of innocence. We have done wrong, thought wrong, wanted wrong things, and encouraged wrong. Sometimes we've only stayed innocent because we failed to carry out our bad intentions.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: When we think of this, let us deal more justly with sinners, and believe that those who scold us are right: in any case let us not be angry with ourselves (for with whom shall we not be angry, if we are angry even with our own selves?), and least of all with the gods: for whatever we suffer befalls us not by any ordinance of theirs but of the common law of all flesh. "But diseases and pains attack us." Well, people who live in a crazy dwelling must have some way of escape from it. Some one will be said to have spoken ill of you: think whether you did not first speak ill of him: think of how many persons you have yourself spoken ill. Let us not, I say, suppose that others are doing us a wrong, but are repaying one which we have done them, that some are acting with good intentions, some under compulsion, some in ignorance, and let us believe that even he who does so intentionally and knowingly did not wrong us merely for the sake of wronging us, but was led into doing so by the attraction of saying something witty, or did whatever he did, not out of any spite against us, but because he himself could not succeed unless he pushed us back.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
When we think about this, let's be fairer to people who sin. And let's accept that those who criticize us might be right. At the very least, let's not be angry with ourselves. After all, if we're angry even with ourselves, who won't we be angry with? And let's especially not be angry with the gods. Whatever we suffer happens not because they ordered it, but because that's just how life works for everyone.

"But we get sick and feel pain." Well, people who live in a falling-down house need some way to get out. Someone will say another person spoke badly of you. Think about whether you didn't speak badly of them first. Think about how many people you yourself have criticized. Let's not assume that others are wronging us. Maybe they're just paying us back for something we did to them first. Some people act with good intentions. Some are forced into it. Some just don't know any better. And even the person who hurts us on purpose — let's believe he didn't do it just to hurt us. Maybe he was tempted by the chance to say something clever. Or maybe he did whatever he did not out of spite toward us, but because he couldn't succeed without pushing us back.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: We are often offended by flattery even while it is being lavished upon us: yet whoever recalls to his mind how often he himself has been the victim of undeserved suspicion, how often fortune has given his true service an appearance of wrong-doing, how many persons he has begun by hating and ended by loving, will be able to keep himself from becoming angry straightway, especially if he silently says to himself when each offence is committed: "I have done this very thing myself." Where, however, will you find so impartial a judge? The same man who lusts after everyone's wife, and thinks that a woman's belonging to someone else is a sufficient reason for adoring her, will not allow any one else to look at his own wife.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: We often get annoyed by flattery even as someone is piling it on us. But think about this: remember how often you've been unfairly suspected of something. Remember how often luck made your good intentions look bad. Remember how many people you started out hating but ended up loving. If you keep these things in mind, you won't get angry so quickly. Especially if you quietly tell yourself when someone offends you: "I've done this exact same thing myself." But where will you find someone fair enough to judge this way? The same man who lusts after everyone else's wife — who thinks a woman belonging to another man is reason enough to want her — won't let anyone even look at his own wife.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: No man expects such exact fidelity as a traitor: the perjurer himself takes vengeance of him who breaks his word: the pettifogging lawyer is most indignant at an action being brought against him: the man who is reckless of his own chastity cannot endure any attempt upon that of his slaves. We have other men's vices before our eyes, and our own behind our backs: hence it is that a father, who is worse than his son, blames the latter for giving extravagant feasts,[10] and disapproves of the least sign of luxury in another, although he was wont to set no bounds to it in his own case; hence it is that despots are angry with homicides, and thefts are punished by those who despoil temples. A great part of mankind is not angry with sins, but with sinners. Regard to our own selves[11] will make us more moderate, if we inquire of ourselves:—have we ever committed any crime of this sort? have we ever fallen into this kind of error? is it for our interest that we should condemn this conduct?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: No one demands more loyalty than a traitor. The man who breaks his own promises gets furious when someone breaks a promise to him. The crooked lawyer gets most upset when someone sues him. The man who cheats on his wife can't stand it when someone makes a move on his slaves. We see other people's faults clearly, but we're blind to our own. That's why a father who's worse than his son will criticize the boy for throwing fancy parties. He'll disapprove of any luxury in others, even though he used to have no limits on his own spending. That's why tyrants get angry at murderers, and temple robbers punish thieves. Most people aren't angry at sins — they're angry at sinners. Looking at ourselves honestly will make us more reasonable. We should ask: Have I ever done something like this? Have I ever made this same mistake? Does it really help me to condemn this behavior?

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
The greatest remedy for anger is delay: beg anger to grant
you this at the first, not in order that it may pardon the offence,
but that it may form a right judgment about it: if it delays, it
will come to an end. Do not attempt to quell it all at once, for
its first impulses are fierce; by plucking away its parts we shall
remove the whole. We are made angry by some things which we learn
at second-hand, and by some which we ourselves hear or see. Now,
we ought to be slow to believe what is told us. Many tell lies in
order to deceive us, and many because they are themselves deceived.
Some seek to win our favour by false accusations, and invent wrongs
in order that they may appear angry at our having suffered them.
One man lies out of spite, that he may set trusting friends at
variance; some because they are suspicious,[12] and wish to see
sport, and watch from a safe distance those whom they have set by
the ears. If you were about to give sentence in court about ever
so small a sum of money, you would take nothing as proved without
a witness, and a witness would count for nothing except on his oath.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
The best cure for anger is time. Ask your anger to give you this at first — not so it will forgive the offense, but so it can judge it properly. If anger waits, it will fade away. Don't try to crush it all at once. Its first rush is fierce. Pick away its pieces and you'll remove the whole thing.

Some things make us angry because we heard them from others. Some things we see or hear ourselves. We should be slow to believe what people tell us. Many people lie to deceive us. Many others lie because they've been deceived themselves. Some try to win our favor with false accusations. They invent wrongs so they can seem angry that we've been hurt. One person lies out of spite to turn trusting friends against each other. Others are suspicious and want to watch the fun from a safe distance after they've stirred up trouble.

If you were giving a court judgment about even a small amount of money, you wouldn't accept anything as fact without a witness. And a witness would mean nothing without an oath.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
You would allow both sides to be heard: you would allow them time:
you would not despatch the matter at one sitting, because the oftener
it is handled the more distinctly the truth appears. And do you
condemn your friend off-hand? Are you angry with him before
you hear his story, before you have cross-examined him, before he
can know either who is his accuser or with what he is charged. Why
then, just now, in the case which you just tried, did you hear what
was said on both sides? This very man who has informed against your
friend, will say no more if he be obliged to prove what he says.
“You need not,” says he, “bring me forward as a witness; if I am
brought forward I shall deny what I have said; unless you excuse
me from appearing I shall never tell you anything.” At the same
time he spurs you on and withdraws himself from the strife and
battle. The man who will tell you nothing save in secret hardly
tells you anything at all. What can be more unjust than to believe
in secret, and to be angry openly?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: You would listen to both sides in court. You would give them time. You wouldn't rush through the case in one session, because the more you examine something, the clearer the truth becomes. So why do you condemn your friend without a hearing? Why are you angry with him before you've heard his side, before you've questioned him, before he even knows who accused him or what the charges are? Just now, in that case you tried, didn't you hear arguments from both sides? This same person who informed against your friend will clam up if he has to prove his claims. "Don't call me as a witness," he'll say. "If you do, I'll deny everything I told you. Unless you promise I won't have to testify, I'll never tell you anything again." He pushes you to act, then pulls himself out of the fight. Someone who will only whisper accusations hardly tells you anything worth knowing. What could be more unfair than believing secret rumors and showing your anger in public?

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Some offences we ourselves witness: in these cases let us
examine the disposition and purpose of the offender. Perhaps he is
a child; let us pardon his youth, he knows not whether he is doing
wrong: or he is a father; he has either rendered such great services,
as to have won the right even to wrong us—or perhaps this very act
which offends us is his chief merit: or a woman; well, she made a
mistake. The man did it because he was ordered to do it. Who but
an unjust person can be angry with what is done under compulsion?
You had hurt him: well, there is no wrong in suffering the pain
which you have been the first to inflict. Suppose that your opponent
is a judge; then you ought to take his opinion rather than your
own: or that he is a king; then, if he punishes the guilty, yield
to him because he is just, and if he punishes the innocent, yield
to him because he is powerful. Suppose that it is a dumb animal or
as stupid as a dumb animal: then, if you are angry with it, you
will make yourself like it. Suppose that it is a disease or a
misfortune; it will take less effect upon you if you bear it quietly:
or that it is a god; then you waste your time by being angry with
him as much as if you prayed him to be angry with some one
else. Is it a good man who has wronged you? do not believe it: is
it a bad one? do not be surprised at this; he will pay to some one
else the penalty which he owes to you—indeed, by his sin he has
already punished himself.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Sometimes we see offenses happen right in front of us. When this happens, let's think about who did it and why. Maybe it's a child — forgive them, they don't know they're doing wrong. Maybe it's a father who has done so much good that he's earned the right to hurt us sometimes. Or maybe this very thing that bothers us is actually his greatest virtue. Maybe it's a woman who simply made a mistake. Maybe the person was just following orders. Who could be angry at someone forced to act? Maybe you hurt him first — well, there's nothing wrong with getting back the pain you started. Suppose your opponent is a judge — then trust his judgment over your own. Or suppose he's a king — if he punishes the guilty, respect his justice. If he punishes the innocent, respect his power. Suppose it's a dumb animal or someone as stupid as one — if you get angry at it, you become just like it. Suppose it's a disease or bad luck — you'll handle it better if you stay calm. Suppose it's a god — then your anger is as pointless as praying for him to get angry at someone else. Is it a good man who wronged you? Don't believe it. Is it a bad man? Don't be surprised. He'll pay someone else the penalty he owes you — in fact, by sinning, he's already punished himself.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: There are, as I have stated, two cases which produce anger: first, when we appear to have received an injury, about which enough has been said, and, secondly, when we appear to have been treated unjustly: this must now be discussed. Men think some things unjust because they ought not to suffer them, and some because they did not expect to suffer them: we think what is unexpected is beneath our deserts. Consequently, we are especially excited at what befalls us contrary to our hope and expectation: and this is why we are irritated at the smallest trifles in our own domestic affairs, and why we call our friends' carelessness deliberate injury. How is it, then, asks our opponent, that we are angered by the injuries inflicted by our enemies? It is because we did not expect those particular injuries, or, at any rate, not on so extensive a scale. This is caused by our excessive self-love: we think that we ought to remain uninjured even by our enemies: every man bears within his breast the mind of a despot, and is willing to commit excesses, but unwilling to submit to them.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: As I said before, two things make us angry. First, when we think someone has hurt us — I've talked enough about that. Second, when we think we've been treated unfairly. That's what I need to discuss now. People call things unfair for two reasons: either they think they shouldn't have to suffer them, or they didn't expect to suffer them. When something catches us off guard, we feel it's beneath what we deserve. That's why we get especially upset when things go against our hopes and expectations. It's why we get irritated by tiny problems at home. It's why we think our friends' thoughtlessness is deliberate cruelty. But wait, someone might ask — why do we get angry when our enemies hurt us? Because we didn't expect those particular attacks, or at least not attacks that bad. This comes from loving ourselves too much. We think we should stay safe even from our enemies. Every person carries the heart of a tyrant inside them. We want the freedom to hurt others, but we don't want to be hurt ourselves.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Thus it is either ignorance or arrogance that makes us angry: ignorance of common facts; for what is there to wonder at in bad men committing evil deeds? what novelty is there in your enemy hurting you, your friend quarrelling with you, your son going wrong, or your servant doing amiss? Fabius was wont to say that the most shameful excuse a general could make was "I did not think." I think it the most shameful excuse that a man can make. Think of everything, expect everything: even with men of good character something queer will crop up; human nature produces minds that are treacherous, ungrateful, greedy, and impious: when you are considering what any man's morals may be, think what those of mankind are. When you are especially enjoying yourself, be especially on your guard: when everything seems to you to be peaceful, be sure that mischief is not absent, but only asleep. Always believe that something will occur to offend you. A pilot never spreads all his canvas abroad so confidently as not to keep his tackle for shortening sail ready for use.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: So anger comes from either ignorance or arrogance. We don't know basic facts about people. Why should you be shocked when bad people do bad things? What's surprising about your enemy hurting you, your friend fighting with you, your son messing up, or your servant making mistakes? The general Fabius used to say the most shameful excuse a commander could give was "I didn't think." I think that's the most shameful excuse anyone can give. Think about everything. Expect everything. Even good people will surprise you with something strange. Human nature creates minds that are sneaky, ungrateful, greedy, and corrupt. When you're judging what any person might do, remember what people in general are like. When you're having the most fun, that's when you need to be most careful. When everything seems peaceful, remember that trouble isn't gone — it's just sleeping. Always believe that something will happen to upset you. A ship captain never puts up all his sails so confidently that he doesn't keep his equipment ready to pull them down quickly.

on-anger_book-2.originalText: Think, above all, how base and hateful is the power of doing mischief, and how unnatural in man, by whose kindness even fierce animals are rendered tame. See how bulls yield their necks to the yoke, how elephants allow boys and women to dance on their backs unhurt, how snakes glide harmlessly over our bosoms and among our drinking-cups, how within their dens bears and lions submit to be handled with complacent mouths, and wild beasts fawn upon their master: let us blush to have exchanged habits with wild beasts. It is a crime to injure one's country: so it is, therefore, to injure any of our countrymen, for he is a part of our country; if the whole be sacred, the parts must be sacred too. Therefore it is also a crime to injure any man: for he is your fellow-citizen in a larger state. What, if the hands were to wish to hurt the feet?
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Think about how ugly and disgusting it is to hurt others. It goes against our very nature as human beings. Our kindness can even tame wild animals. Look how bulls let us put yokes on their necks. Elephants let children and women dance safely on their backs. Snakes slide harmlessly across our chests and around our cups. In their dens, bears and lions let us pet them with gentle mouths. Wild beasts show affection to their masters. We should be ashamed that we've become worse than wild animals. It's a crime to hurt your country. So it's also a crime to hurt any of your countrymen, because each person is part of your country. If the whole thing is sacred, then the parts must be sacred too. Therefore, it's also a crime to hurt any human being. Every person is your fellow citizen in the larger community of humanity. What if your hands decided to hurt your feet?

on-anger_book-2.originalText: or the eyes to hurt the hands? As all the limbs act in unison, because it is the interest of the whole body to keep each one of them safe, so men should spare one another, because they are born for society. The bond of society, however, cannot exist unless it guards and loves all its members. We should not even destroy vipers and water-snakes and other creatures whose teeth and claws are dangerous, if we were able to tame them as we do other animals, or to prevent their being a peril to us: neither ought we, therefore, to hurt a man because he has done wrong, but lest he should do wrong, and our punishment should always look to the future, and never to the past, because it is inflicted in a spirit of precaution, not of anger: for if everyone who has a crooked and vicious disposition were to be punished, no one would escape punishment.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Would your eyes ever try to hurt your hands? All your body parts work together because the whole body benefits when each part stays safe. People should spare each other for the same reason — we're born to live together. Society can only work if it protects and cares for all its members. We don't even kill vipers and water snakes and other dangerous creatures if we can tame them like other animals, or keep them from harming us. So we shouldn't hurt a person because he did something wrong, but only to prevent him from doing wrong again. Our punishment should always look forward, never backward. We punish to be careful, not because we're angry. If we punished everyone with a twisted and wicked nature, no one would escape punishment.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“But anger possesses a certain pleasure of its own, and it
is sweet to pay back the pain you have suffered.” Not at all; it
is not honourable to requite injuries by injuries, in the same way
as it is to repay benefits by benefits. In the latter case it is a
shame to be conquered; in the former it is a shame to conquer.
Revenge and retaliation are words which men use and even think to
be righteous, yet they do not greatly differ from wrong-doing,
except in the order in which they are done: he who renders pain for
pain has more excuse for his sin; that is all. Some one who did not
know Marcus Cato struck him in the public bath in his ignorance,
for who would knowingly have done him an injury? Afterwards when
he was apologizing, Cato replied, “I do not remember being struck.”
He thought it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it. You
ask, “Did no harm befall that man for his insolence?” No, but rather
much good; he made the acquaintance of Cato. It is the part of a
great mind to despise wrongs done to it; the most contemptuous form
of revenge is not to deem one’s adversary worth taking vengeance
upon. Many have taken small injuries much more seriously to heart
than they need, by revenging them: that man is great and noble who
like a large wild animal hears unmoved the tiny curs that bark at
him.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
"But anger has its own pleasure, and it feels sweet to pay back the pain you've suffered." Not at all. It's not honorable to answer injuries with injuries, just as it is honorable to repay good deeds with good deeds. In one case, it's shameful to be beaten. In the other, it's shameful to win. Revenge and retaliation are words people use and even think are righteous. But they're not much different from wrongdoing — just done in a different order. The person who returns pain for pain has more excuse for his sin. That's all.

Someone who didn't know Marcus Cato once struck him at the public bath out of ignorance. Who would have hurt him on purpose? Later, when the man was apologizing, Cato said, "I don't remember being struck." He thought it was better to ignore the insult than to get revenge.

You ask, "Did that man face no consequences for his rudeness?" No. But he gained something much better — he got to meet Cato.

It's the mark of a great mind to dismiss wrongs done against it. The most scornful form of revenge is to decide your enemy isn't worth taking revenge on. Many people have taken small injuries far more seriously than needed by getting revenge. That person is great and noble who, like a large wild animal, listens unmoved to the tiny dogs that bark at him.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“We are treated,” says our opponent, “with more respect if
we revenge our injuries.” If we make use of revenge merely as a
remedy, let us use it without anger, and not regard revenge as
pleasant, but as useful: yet often it is better to pretend not to
have received an injury than to avenge it. The wrongs of the powerful
must not only be borne, but borne with a cheerful countenance: they
will repeat the wrong if they think they have inflicted it. This
is the worst trait of minds rendered arrogant by prosperity,
they hate those whom they have injured. Every one knows the saying
of the old courtier, who, when some one asked him how he had achieved
the rare distinction of living at court till he reached old age,
replied, “By receiving wrongs and returning thanks for them.” It
is often so far from expedient to avenge our wrongs, that it will
not do even to admit them. Gaius Caesar, offended at the smart
clothes and well-dressed hair of the son of Pastor, a distinguished
Roman knight, sent him to prison. When the father begged that his
son might suffer no harm, Caius, as if reminded by this to put him
to death, ordered him to be executed, yet, in order to mitigate his
brutality to the father, invited him that very day to dinner. Pastor
came with a countenance which betrayed no illwill. Caesar pledged
him in a glass of wine, and set a man to watch him. The wretched
creature went through his part, feeling as though he were drinking
his son’s blood: the emperor sent him some perfume and a garland,
and gave orders to watch whether he used them: he did so.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: "People respect us more," our opponent says, "when we get revenge for wrongs done to us." Fine. If we use revenge as medicine, let's do it without anger. Don't think of revenge as fun — think of it as useful. But often it's better to pretend you didn't notice the injury at all than to strike back. When powerful people wrong you, you must not only put up with it — you must look happy about it. If they think they hurt you, they'll do it again. This is the worst thing about minds made arrogant by success: they hate the people they've injured. Everyone knows the story of the old courtier. Someone asked him how he managed to survive at court until old age. He replied, "By accepting wrongs and thanking people for them." Often it's not just unwise to avenge wrongs — it won't even work to admit they happened. Caius Caesar was annoyed by Pastor's son, a distinguished Roman knight, because the young man dressed too well and styled his hair nicely. So Caesar threw him in prison. When Pastor begged that his son be spared, Caius — as if suddenly reminded to kill him — ordered his execution. But to soften this cruelty to the father, Caesar invited Pastor to dinner that very day. Pastor came with a face that showed no anger. Caesar toasted him with wine and had someone watch his reaction. The miserable man played his part, feeling as if he were drinking his own son's blood. The emperor sent him perfume and a garland, and ordered his men to watch whether Pastor would use them. He did.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
On the
very day on which he had buried, nay, on which he had not even
buried his son, he sat down as one of a hundred guests, and, old
and gouty as he was, drank to an extent which would have been hardly
decent on a child’s birthday; he shed no tear the while; he did not
permit his grief to betray itself by the slightest sign; he dined
just as though his entreaties had gained his son’s life. You ask
me why he did so? he had another son. What did Priam do in the
Iliad? Did he not conceal his wrath and embrace the knees of Achilles?
did he not raise to his lips that death-dealing hand, stained with
the blood of his son, and sup with his slayer? True! but there were
no perfumes and garlands, and his fierce enemy encouraged him with
many soothing words to eat, not to drain huge goblets with a guard
standing over him to see that he did it. Had he only feared for
himself, the father would have treated the tyrant with scorn:
but love for his son quenched his anger: he deserved the emperor’s
permission to leave the banquet and gather up the bones of his son:
but, meanwhile, that kindly and polite youth the emperor would not
even permit him to do this, but tormented the old man with frequent
invitations to drink, advising him thereby to lighten his sorrows.
He, on the other hand, appeared to be in good spirits, and to have
forgotten what had been done that day: he would have lost his second
son had he proved an unacceptable guest to the murderer of his
eldest.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
On the very day he buried his son — no, on the day he hadn't even been allowed to bury his son yet — this man sat down as one of a hundred dinner guests. Old and suffering from gout, he drank more than would be proper even at a child's birthday party. He shed no tears. He didn't let his grief show by even the smallest sign. He dined as if his pleading had actually saved his son's life. You ask why he did this? He had another son.

What did Priam do in the Iliad? Didn't he hide his rage and kneel before Achilles? Didn't he kiss the very hand that killed his son, stained with his boy's blood, and eat dinner with his son's killer? Yes, but there were no fancy perfumes and flower garlands at that meal. And his fierce enemy spoke kindly, gently encouraging him to eat — not forcing him to drain huge cups while a guard watched to make sure he did it.

If this father had only feared for himself, he would have treated the tyrant with contempt. But love for his son crushed his anger. He deserved the emperor's permission to leave the banquet and collect his son's bones. But that 'kind and polite' young emperor wouldn't even allow him this. Instead, he tormented the old man with constant invitations to drink, telling him it would ease his sorrow.

The father appeared to be in good spirits, as if he had forgotten what happened that day. If he had been a poor guest to his eldest son's murderer, he would have lost his second son too.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
We must, therefore, refrain from anger, whether he who
provokes us be on a level with ourselves, or above us, or below us.
A contest with one’s equal is of uncertain issue, with one’s superior
is folly, and with one’s inferior is contemptible. It is the part
of a mean and wretched man to turn and bite one’s biter: even mice
and ants show their teeth if you put your hand to them, and all
feeble creatures think that they are hurt if they are touched. It
will make us milder tempered to call to mind any services which he
with whom we are angry may have done us, and to let his deserts
balance his offence. Let us also reflect, how much credit the tale
of our forgiveness will confer upon us, how many men may be made
into valuable friends by forgiveness. One of the lessons which
Sulla’s cruelty teaches us is not to be angry with the children of
our enemies, whether they be public or private; for he drove the
sons of the proscribed into exile. Nothing is more unjust than that
any one should inherit the quarrels of his father.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: So we must avoid anger, whether the person provoking us is our equal, our superior, or our inferior. Fighting with an equal could go either way. Fighting with someone above you is stupid. Fighting with someone below you is disgraceful. Only a petty, miserable person bites back when bitten. Even mice and ants will bare their teeth if you reach for them. All weak creatures think they're being hurt when you just touch them. We'll be calmer if we remember the good things that person has done for us. Let their past kindness balance out their current offense. Also think about this: how much respect we'll earn by forgiving them. How many enemies we could turn into valuable friends through forgiveness. Sulla's cruelty teaches us one lesson — don't stay angry at your enemies' children, whether in public or private life. He sent the sons of executed men into exile. Nothing is more unfair than making someone inherit their father's quarrels.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Whenever we are
loth to pardon any one, let us think whether it would be to our
advantage that all men should be inexorable. He who refuses to
pardon, how often has he begged it for himself? how often has he
grovelled at the feet of those whom he spurns from his own? How can
we gain more glory than by turning anger into friendship?
what more faithful allies has the Roman people than those who have
been its most unyielding enemies? where would the empire be to-day,
had not a wise foresight united the conquered and the conquerors?
If any one is angry with you, meet his anger by returning benefits
for it: a quarrel which is only taken up on one side falls to the
ground: it takes two men to fight. But[14] suppose that there is
an angry struggle on both sides, even then, he is the better man
who first gives way; the winner is the real loser. He struck you;
well then, do you fall back: if you strike him in turn you will
give him both an opportunity and an excuse for striking you again:
you will not be able to withdraw yourself from the struggle when
you please.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: When we don't want to forgive someone, we should ask ourselves: would we want everyone to be unforgiving toward us? The person who won't forgive others — how many times has he begged for forgiveness himself? How often has he groveled at the feet of people he now pushes away? What brings us more honor than turning an enemy into a friend? Rome's most loyal allies are the nations that once fought us most fiercely. Where would our empire be today if we hadn't wisely united our former enemies with ourselves? If someone is angry with you, respond with kindness instead. A fight needs two people — if only one person is fighting, there's no fight at all. But let's say both sides are angry and struggling. Even then, whoever backs down first is the better person. The "winner" is actually the real loser. He hit you? Step back. If you hit him back, you give him both a chance and a reason to hit you again. Once you're in that cycle, you won't be able to get out when you want to.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Does any one wish to strike his enemy so hard, as to leave
his own hand in the wound, and not to be able to recover his balance
after the blow? yet such a weapon is anger: it is scarcely possible
to draw it back. We are careful to choose for ourselves light
weapons, handy and manageable swords: shall we not avoid these
clumsy, unwieldy,[15] and never-to-be-recalled impulses of the mind?
The only swiftness of which men approve is that which, when bidden,
checks itself and proceeds no further, and which can be guided, and
reduced from a run to a walk: we know that the sinews are diseased
when they move against our will. A man must be either aged or weakly
who runs when he wants to walk: let us think that those are the
most powerful and the soundest operations of our minds, which act
under our own control, not at their own caprice. Nothing, however,
will be of so much service as to consider, first, the hideousness,
and, secondly, the danger of anger. No passion bears a more troubled
aspect: it befouls the fairest face, makes fierce the expression
which before was peaceful. From the angry “all grace has fled;”
though their clothing may be fashionable, they will trail it
on the ground and take no heed of their appearance; though their
hair be smoothed down in a comely manner by nature or art, yet it
will bristle up in sympathy with their mind.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Would anyone want to hit their enemy so hard that their own hand gets stuck in the wound? Would anyone want to throw such a wild punch that they lose their balance and fall down? Yet that's exactly what anger is like. Once you let it fly, it's almost impossible to pull it back. We carefully choose light, easy-to-handle weapons when we fight. So why don't we avoid these clumsy, uncontrollable attacks of the mind? The only speed we admire is the kind that stops when we tell it to. We want movements we can guide and slow down from a run to a walk. When our muscles move against our will, we know something is wrong with them. A man who runs when he wants to walk must be old or sick. The strongest and healthiest operations of our mind are the ones we control ourselves, not the ones that act on their own whims. But nothing will help you more than thinking about two things: first, how ugly anger is, and second, how dangerous it is. No other emotion looks more disturbing. It ruins the most beautiful face and turns a peaceful expression fierce. All grace disappears from angry people. Even if their clothes are stylish, they'll drag them on the ground and stop caring how they look. Even if their hair is perfectly styled, it will stand on end to match their wild mind.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
The veins become
swollen, the breast will be shaken by quick breathing, the man’s
neck will be swelled as he roars forth his frantic talk: then, too,
his limbs will tremble, his hands will be restless, his whole body
will sway hither and thither. What, think you, must be the state
of his mind within him, when its appearance without is so shocking?
how far more dreadful a countenance he bears within his own breast,
how far keener pride, how much more violent rage, which will burst
him unless it finds some vent? Let us paint anger looking like those
who are dripping with the blood of foemen or savage beasts, or those
who are just about to slaughter them—like those monsters of the
nether world fabled by the poet to be girt with serpents and breathing
flame, when they sally forth from hell, most frightful to behold,
in order that they may kindle wars, stir up strife between nations,
and overthrow peace; let us paint her eyes glowing with fire, her
voice hissing, roaring, grating, and making worse sounds if worse
there be, while she brandishes weapons in both hands, for she cares
not to protect herself, gloomy, stained with blood, covered with
scars and livid with her own blows, reeling like a maniac, wrapped
in a thick cloud, dashing hither and thither, spreading desolation
and panic, loathed by every one and by herself above all, willing,
if otherwise she cannot hurt her foe, to overthrow alike earth,
sea, and heaven, harmful and hateful at the same time. Or, if we
are to see her, let her be such as our poets have described her—
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: The veins swell up. The chest heaves with quick, sharp breaths. The man's neck bulges as he screams out his wild words. His limbs shake, his hands won't stay still, his whole body rocks back and forth. What do you think his mind must look like inside, when what we see on the outside is so terrible? How much more awful the face he wears inside his chest — how much fiercer his pride, how much more violent his rage, which will tear him apart unless it finds some way out? Let's picture anger looking like those warriors dripping with the blood of enemies or wild beasts, or like those about to kill. Picture her like those monsters from hell that poets describe — wrapped in serpents and breathing fire, when they come up from the underworld looking terrifying, ready to start wars, stir up fights between nations, and destroy peace. Let's paint her eyes glowing with fire, her voice hissing, roaring, grinding, making sounds even worse if there are any. She waves weapons in both hands, not caring to protect herself. She's dark, stained with blood, covered with scars and bruises from her own blows. She staggers like a madwoman, wrapped in thick clouds, charging back and forth, spreading ruin and terror. Everyone hates her, and she hates herself most of all. If she can't hurt her enemy any other way, she's willing to destroy earth, sea, and sky all at once. She's both harmful and hateful. Or if we're going to see her, let her be just as our poets have described her —

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
“There with her blood-stained scourge Bellona fights. And
Discord in her riven robe delights,”[16]

or, if possible, let some even more dreadful aspect be invented
for this dreadful passion.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish:
"There with her blood-stained whip Bellona fights. And Discord in her torn robe delights,"

or, if possible, let someone invent an even more terrifying image for this terrifying passion.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Some angry people, as Sextius remarks, have been benefited
by looking at the glass: they have been struck by so great an
alteration in their own appearance: they have been, as it were,
brought into their own presence and have not recognized themselves:
yet how small a part of the real hideousness of anger did that
reflected image in the mirror reproduce? Could the mind be displayed
or made to appear through any substance, we should be confounded
when we beheld how black and stained, how agitated, distorted, and
swollen it looked: even at present it is very ugly when seen through
all the screens of blood, bones, and so forth: what would it be,
were it displayed uncovered? You say, that you do not believe that
any one was ever scared out of anger by a mirror: and why not?
Because when he came to the mirror to change his mind, he had changed
it already: to angry men no face looks fairer than one that is
fierce and savage and such as they wish to look like. We ought
rather to consider, how many men anger itself has injured. Some in
their excessive heat have burst their veins; some by straining their
voices beyond their strength have vomited blood, or have injured
their sight by too violently injecting humours into their eyes, and
have fallen sick when the fit passed off. No way leads more swiftly
to madness: many have, consequently, remained always in the frenzy
of anger, and, having once lost their reason, have never recovered
it.
on-anger_book-2.plainEnglish: Some angry people, as Sextius points out, have been helped by looking in a mirror. They were shocked by how much their appearance had changed. It was like meeting themselves face to face and not recognizing who they saw. But even then, the mirror only showed a tiny fraction of how hideous anger really makes us look. If we could see the mind itself — if it could be displayed through some kind of substance — we would be horrified. We'd see how black and stained it looks, how agitated and twisted and swollen. Even now, hidden behind all our blood and bones and flesh, the mind is very ugly when angry. What would it look like if we could see it completely uncovered? You might say you don't believe anyone was ever scared out of anger by looking in a mirror. But why not? Because by the time someone goes to the mirror wanting to change their mind, they've already changed it. To angry people, no face looks better than one that is fierce and savage — the kind of face they want to have. We should think instead about how many people anger itself has actually hurt. Some have gotten so overheated that they burst their blood vessels. Others strained their voices so hard they vomited blood, or damaged their eyesight by forcing too much fluid into their eyes. They got sick when the anger finally passed. No path leads to madness faster than this one. Many people have stayed trapped in angry frenzy forever. Once they lost their reason, they never got it back.

on-anger_book-2.originalText:
Ajax was driven mad by anger, and driven to suicide by madness.
Men, frantic with rage, call upon heaven to slay their children,
to reduce themselves to poverty, and to ruin their houses, and yet
declare that they are not either angry or insane. Enemies to their
best friends, dangerous to their nearest and dearest, regardless
of the laws save where they injure, swayed by the smallest trifles,
unwilling to lend their ears to the advice or the services
of their friends, they do everything by main force, and are ready
either to fight with their swords or to throw themselves upon them,
for the greatest of all evils, and one which surpasses all vices,
has gained possession of them. Other passions gain a footing in the
mind by slow degrees: anger’s conquest is sudden and complete, and,
moreover, it makes all other passions subservient to itself. It
conquers the warmest love: men have thrust swords through the bodies
